beginner.content:
What is Web Architecture?

• Web architecture defines how different components of a web application interact with each other.


Client–Server Model

  • • Client: Browser or mobile app that sends requests.
  • • Server: Machine that processes requests and sends responses.

How It Works

  1. • User enters URL in browser.
  2. • Browser sends HTTP request to server.
  3. • Server processes request.
  4. • Server sends HTTP response.
  5. • Browser displays the result.

Example

• You open www.google.com. Your browser (client) sends request to Google server. Server responds with HTML page.

HTTP Request & Response

  • • Request: Sent by client (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
  • • Response: Sent by server (Status code + Data)

Status Codes

  • • 200 – Success
  • • 404 – Not Found
  • • 500 – Server Error

Fresher Notes

  • Client (browser or app) sends a request; the server processes it and returns a response, and the two talk over a network using a protocol.
  • Tiers: presentation (HTML in the browser), business logic (servlets, services) and data (database) are kept in separate layers.
  • Stateless web: the server does not remember you between requests unless you use cookies or a session.

Worked Example 1

Layered code: servlet to service to DAO.

Worked Example 2

Inspect where a request goes with curl.

Practice Exercise 1

Simple client in Java: talk to a server with a raw socket.

Practice Exercise 2

Tiny server: one tier answers every client.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A request crosses several layers before your code runs.

  • DNS: the name is resolved to an IP address and cached.
  • TCP: a three-way handshake opens the connection; TLS adds more round trips.
  • Server: a connector thread reads bytes and the container builds request objects.
  • Pipeline: filters, then the servlet, then the response travels back on the same connection.
  • Keep-alive: the connection stays open for the next request.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common deployment shapes:

  • Single server: browser to Tomcat to database; simple, one point of failure.
  • Reverse proxy: Nginx in front for TLS and static files.
  • Load balanced: several Tomcat nodes behind a balancer.
  • Microservices: small services each with its own database, called over HTTP.
  • CDN: static content served near the user.

intermediate.content:
3-Tier Architecture

Most modern web apps use 3 layers:

  • • Presentation Layer: Frontend (React, Angular)
  • • Business Logic Layer: Backend (Spring Boot, .NET)
  • • Data Layer: Database (MySQL, MongoDB)

This separation improves maintainability and scalability.

Stateless vs Stateful

  • • Stateless: Each request is independent (REST APIs).
  • • Stateful: Server stores session data.

REST Architecture

  • • Uses HTTP methods properly.
  • • Stateless communication.
  • • Resource-based URLs.

Middleware Concept

• Middleware acts between request and response.

  • • Authentication middleware
  • • Logging middleware
  • • Error handling middleware

Example: In Spring Boot, filters and interceptors act as middleware.

Session Management

  • • Cookies
  • • Session ID
  • • JWT Token

JWT is commonly used in modern stateless applications.
codeExamples:
// Example JWT Authorization Header
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9

intermediate.content:
Client-Side Rendering vs Server-Side Rendering

  • • CSR: Rendering happens in browser (React).
  • • SSR: Rendering happens on server (Next.js).

SSR improves SEO and initial load performance.

Database Connection Flow

App Server communicates with database using:

  • • Connection Pool
  • • ORM (Hibernate, Entity Framework)

Connection pooling improves performance.

expert.content:
Microservices Architecture

• Instead of one big server (Monolith), application is divided into small independent services.


Advantages

  • • Independent deployment
  • • Scalable services
  • • Better fault isolation

Challenges

  • • Service communication (REST, gRPC)
  • • Distributed transactions
  • • Monitoring & logging

API Gateway Pattern

• Single entry point for all client requests in microservices architecture.

  • • Authentication
  • • Rate limiting
  • • Request routing
  • • Load balancing

Event-Driven Architecture

• Services communicate via events using message brokers.

  • • Kafka
  • • RabbitMQ
  • • ActiveMQ

• Improves scalability and decouples services.
codeExamples:
// Example: Publishing event (Pseudo code)
eventPublisher.publish("order-created", orderData);

expert.content:
Distributed Systems Concepts

  • • CAP Theorem (Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance)
  • • Eventual Consistency
  • • Circuit Breaker Pattern

• Tools: Resilience4j, Hystrix

Containerization & Deployment

  • • Docker for containerization
  • • Kubernetes for orchestration
  • • CI/CD pipelines for automated deployment
codeExamples:
# Example Dockerfile
FROM openjdk:17
COPY target/app.jar app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app.jar"]

expert.content:
Advanced Caching Strategies

  • • Cache Aside Pattern
  • • Write Through Cache
  • • Distributed Cache (Redis Cluster)

Security in Distributed Architecture

  • • OAuth 2.0
  • • OpenID Connect
  • • API Rate Limiting
  • • Zero Trust Architecture

• Security must be applied at every layer.

Observability & Monitoring

  • • Centralized Logging (ELK Stack)
  • • Metrics Monitoring (Prometheus, Grafana)
  • • Distributed Tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin)

• Helps identify bottlenecks and failures in distributed systems.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Thin and thick client: a browser page is a thin client; a single-page app moves more logic into the browser and calls JSON APIs.
  • Scaling: put a load balancer in front of several identical app servers; keep them stateless or share session data.
  • Static versus dynamic: static files (images, CSS) can be served by a web server or CDN; dynamic pages need a servlet container.

Senior Notes

  • Reverse proxy: Nginx or a cloud gateway terminates TLS, caches, compresses and forwards to Tomcat on a private port.
  • Session strategy: sticky sessions, a shared store such as Redis, or stateless tokens (JWT) decide how well you scale out.
  • Failure thinking: every network call can time out, so set timeouts, retries and health checks at each tier.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical architecture mistakes:

  • Business logic in JSP: move it to services.
  • Storing big objects in the session: memory grows per user; keep ids only.
  • No timeouts: a slow database blocks all threads; set connection and read timeouts.
  • Trusting the client: always validate on the server, since the browser can be bypassed.
  • Chatty calls: many small remote calls instead of one coarse call.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance levers by tier:

  • Browser: cache headers, compression, fewer requests.
  • Edge: CDN and HTTP/2.
  • App: thread pool size, connection pool, avoiding blocking calls.
  • Data: indexes, caching of hot reads.
  • Measure first: use percentiles (p95, p99), not averages.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a shop slows down on sale days. Fixes by tier:

  • Static images move to a CDN.
  • Tomcat nodes scale from one to three behind a balancer, with sessions in Redis.
  • Product reads are cached for 60 seconds.
  • A health endpoint lets the balancer remove a sick node automatically.

beginner.content:
What is HTTP?

• HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a communication protocol used between client (browser) and server.

  • • It is used to transfer web pages.
  • • Works on Port 80 by default.
  • • It is stateless (each request is independent).

How HTTP Works

  1. • Client sends HTTP request.
  2. • Server processes request.
  3. • Server sends HTTP response.

What is HTTPS?

• HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) is the secure version of HTTP.

  • • Uses SSL/TLS encryption.
  • • Works on Port 443.
  • • Encrypts data between client and server.

• HTTPS protects sensitive data like passwords, credit card details.

HTTP vs HTTPS (Basic Difference)

HTTP HTTPS
Not Secure Secure (Encrypted)
Port 80 Port 443
No Encryption Uses SSL/TLS

Fresher Notes

  • HTTP is a text request-response protocol on top of TCP; default port is 80 and for HTTPS it is 443.
  • Methods: GET reads, POST creates or submits, PUT replaces, DELETE removes.
  • HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS, so the traffic is encrypted and the server is verified by a certificate.

Worked Example 1

Read request line and headers in a servlet.

Worked Example 2

Redirect HTTP to HTTPS.

Practice Exercise 1

A raw HTTP request and response.

Practice Exercise 2

Send a POST with curl.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

HTTP/1.1 is plain text on a TCP stream, and TLS wraps it for HTTPS.

  • Framing: the body length comes from Content-Length or chunked encoding.
  • Handshake: ClientHello, ServerHello with certificate, key exchange, then encrypted data.
  • Certificate: signed by a certificate authority; the client checks the chain and host name.
  • Keep-alive: one connection serves many requests.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Methods and status codes to know:

  • GET, HEAD: safe reads.
  • POST: create or run an action.
  • PUT, PATCH: replace or partly update.
  • DELETE: remove.
  • 200, 201, 204: success variants.
  • 301, 302, 304: redirect and not-modified.
  • 400, 401, 403, 404, 409: client problems.
  • 500, 502, 503: server problems.

intermediate.content:
HTTP Request Structure

  • • Request Line (GET /index.html HTTP/1.1)
  • • Headers (Content-Type, Authorization)
  • • Body (Data for POST/PUT requests)
codeExamples:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "ashish@gmail.com",
  "password": "123456"
}

intermediate.content:
HTTP Response Structure

  • • Status Line (HTTP/1.1 200 OK)
  • • Headers
  • • Body

Common Status Codes

  • • 200 – OK
  • • 201 – Created
  • • 400 – Bad Request
  • • 401 – Unauthorized
  • • 404 – Not Found
  • • 500 – Internal Server Error

SSL/TLS Handshake (HTTPS Working)

When using HTTPS:

  1. • Client sends request to server.
  2. • Server sends SSL certificate.
  3. • Client verifies certificate.
  4. • Encryption key is generated.
  5. • Secure communication begins.

HTTP Methods

  • • GET – Retrieve data
  • • POST – Send data
  • • PUT – Update data
  • • DELETE – Remove data
  • • PATCH – Partial update

HTTP Headers Deep Dive

• Headers provide additional information about the request or response.


Important Request Headers

  • • Authorization
  • • Content-Type
  • • Accept
  • • User-Agent
  • • Cookie

Important Response Headers

  • • Set-Cookie
  • • Cache-Control
  • • Location
  • • Content-Encoding
codeExamples:
GET /profile HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9

intermediate.content:
Cookies & Sessions

  • • Cookies store small data in browser.
  • • Session ID is stored in cookie.
  • • Server maintains session data.

• Modern apps use JWT instead of traditional sessions.
codeExamples: Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=ABC123; HttpOnly; Secure

intermediate.content:
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)

• CORS controls which domains can access your API.

  • • Prevents unauthorized cross-origin requests.
  • • Uses headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
codeExamples: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://myfrontend.com

intermediate.content:
Idempotent vs Non-Idempotent Methods

  • • Idempotent: GET, PUT, DELETE (multiple calls same result)
  • • Non-Idempotent: POST (creates new resource each time)

This concept is important in REST API design.

HTTP Caching Mechanism

  • • ETag
  • • Last-Modified
  • • Cache-Control
  • • Expires

• Caching reduces server load and improves performance.
codeExamples: Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600

expert.content:
HTTP Versions

  • • HTTP/1.1: Text-based, supports persistent connections.
  • • HTTP/2: Binary protocol, multiplexing, header compression.
  • • HTTP/3: Uses QUIC (UDP-based), faster and more secure.

• HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 improve performance significantly.

Advanced HTTPS Security Concepts

  • • Symmetric Encryption
  • • Asymmetric Encryption
  • • Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)
  • • Certificate Authorities (CA)
  • • Digital Signatures

Security Attacks Related to HTTP

  • • Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)
  • • SSL Stripping
  • • Session Hijacking
  • • Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

• HTTPS helps prevent many of these attacks.

HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)

• HSTS forces browsers to use HTTPS only.

• This prevents downgrade attacks and improves security.
codeExamples: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

expert.content:
Performance Optimization in HTTP

  • • Keep-Alive Connections
  • • Compression (Gzip, Brotli)
  • • CDN Usage
  • • HTTP Caching Headers (ETag, Cache-Control)

TLS Encryption Internals

• HTTPS uses both asymmetric and symmetric encryption:

  • • Asymmetric encryption for key exchange.
  • • Symmetric encryption for data transfer.

• This ensures both security and performance.

Certificate Types

  • • Domain Validation (DV)
  • • Organization Validation (OV)
  • • Extended Validation (EV)
  • • Wildcard Certificates
  • • Self-Signed Certificates

• Production systems should use CA-issued certificates.

Mutual TLS (mTLS)

• Both client and server authenticate each other using certificates.

  • • Used in microservices architecture
  • • Enhances security in internal APIs

HTTP/2 Advanced Features

  • • Multiplexing (multiple requests in single connection)
  • • Header compression (HPACK)
  • • Server Push

• Improves latency and performance significantly.

QUIC & HTTP/3

  • • Uses UDP instead of TCP
  • • Faster handshake
  • • Built-in encryption

• Reduces connection establishment time.

Security Best Practices

  • • Always redirect HTTP → HTTPS
  • • Use HSTS
  • • Enable Secure & HttpOnly cookies
  • • Disable weak TLS versions
  • • Use strong cipher suites

Common Real-World Production Setup

• Client → CDN → Load Balancer → Reverse Proxy (Nginx) → App Server → Database

  • • SSL termination at Load Balancer
  • • Internal traffic secured with mTLS
  • • WAF (Web Application Firewall) protection

Mid-Level Notes

  • Status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (404), 5xx server error (500).
  • Safe and idempotent: GET is safe, and PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so repeating them gives the same result.
  • Headers carry metadata such as Content-Type, Cookie, Cache-Control and Authorization.

Senior Notes

  • TLS handshake: client and server agree on a cipher, the server proves its identity with a certificate chain, and session keys are derived.
  • HTTP versions: HTTP/1.1 uses keep-alive; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
  • Security headers: Strict-Transport-Security, Secure and HttpOnly cookie flags reduce attacks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Sensitive data in GET URLs: they appear in logs and history; use POST.
  • Changing data with GET: crawlers and prefetch can trigger it.
  • Mixed content: an HTTPS page loading HTTP scripts is blocked.
  • Missing Secure flag: a session cookie can leak over HTTP.
  • Ignoring character encoding: call setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8") before reading parameters.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning HTTP:

  • Cache validators: ETag and Last-Modified return cheap 304 answers.
  • Compression: gzip text responses.
  • HTTP/2: fewer connections and header compression.
  • TLS session resumption cuts handshake cost.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: moving a site to HTTPS. Steps:

  • Get a certificate and configure TLS at the proxy or Connector.
  • Redirect all HTTP traffic with 301.
  • Add the HSTS header.
  • Fix mixed content and mark cookies Secure.
codeExamples:
<Connector port="8443" protocol="org.apache.coyote.http11.Http11NioProtocol"
           SSLEnabled="true" scheme="https" secure="true">
  <SSLHostConfig>
    <Certificate certificateKeystoreFile="conf/keystore.p12"
                 certificateKeystorePassword="changeit" type="RSA" />
  </SSLHostConfig>
</Connector>

// OUTPUT:
// https://localhost:8443/shop/ serves the app over TLS

beginner.content:
Introduction to HTTP Request–Response Cycle

• The HTTP Request–Response cycle is the communication process between a client (browser) and a server.

• Every time you open a website, this cycle happens behind the scenes.


Basic Steps

  1. • User enters URL
  2. • Browser sends HTTP request
  3. • Server processes request
  4. • Server sends HTTP response
  5. • Browser renders content

Understanding HTTP Request

• An HTTP request is sent by the client to ask for data or perform an action.

  • • Method – GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
  • • URL – Resource path
  • • Headers – Metadata
  • • Body – Data (for POST/PUT)
codeExamples:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "user@gmail.com",
  "password": "123456"
}

beginner.content:
Understanding HTTP Response

• The server sends a response after processing the request.

  • • Status Code
  • • Response Headers
  • • Response Body

Fresher Notes

  • Cycle: the client opens a connection, sends a request line, headers and optional body, and the server replies with a status line, headers and body.
  • Request parts: method, URL (path and query string), HTTP version, headers and body.
  • Response parts: status code, headers (for example Content-Type) and the body.

Worked Example 1

Forward versus redirect.

Worked Example 2

Log every request phase.

Practice Exercise 1

Raw cycle with a form post.

Practice Exercise 2

Timing phases with curl.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Inside the container, one request goes through fixed stages.

  • Accept: the connector accepts the socket and a worker thread parses the request.
  • Map: host, context and servlet are chosen from the URL.
  • Filter chain: filters run before and after the servlet.
  • Service: service() calls doGet or doPost.
  • Commit: the response is flushed and the thread returns to the pool.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to write the response:

  • getWriter(): text.
  • getOutputStream(): binary data; you cannot use both in one response.
  • setStatus, sendError: status and error page.
  • sendRedirect: 302.
  • Headers: setHeader, addHeader.

intermediate.content:
DNS Resolution

• Before sending request, browser converts domain name into IP address using DNS.

Example: example.com → 93.184.216.34
codeExamples:
// Check DNS via command line
nslookup example.com

intermediate.content:
TCP Connection (3-Way Handshake)

• Before HTTP data transfer, TCP connection is established.

  • • SYN
  • • SYN-ACK
  • • ACK
codeExamples:
// View open TCP connections
netstat -an | find "443"

intermediate.content:
Server-Side Processing Flow

• Once request reaches server:

  • • Passes through Filters
  • • Authentication check
  • • Controller handles request
  • • Service executes logic
  • • Database interaction

Database Interaction

• Application server communicates with database to fetch/store data.

Browser Rendering Process

• After receiving response:

  • • Parse HTML
  • • Build DOM
  • • Load CSS
  • • Execute JavaScript
  • • Render page
codeExamples: Hello World

intermediate.content:
State Management in HTTP

• HTTP is stateless, so sessions or tokens maintain state.
codeExamples:
// Example Cookie Header
Set-Cookie: sessionId=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure

expert.content:
HTTPS & TLS Handshake

• For secure communication:

  1. • Client Hello
  2. • Server Hello
  3. • Certificate exchange
  4. • Key exchange
  5. • Encrypted communication
codeExamples:
// Check SSL certificate
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443

expert.content:
Reverse Proxy Architecture

• Production flow:

• Client → CDN → Load Balancer → Nginx → App Server → DB

HTTP/2 & Multiplexing

• HTTP/2 allows multiple parallel requests over single connection.
codeExamples:
# Enable HTTP/2 in Nginx
listen 443 ssl http2;

expert.content:
Distributed Tracing

• Each request carries unique Trace ID across microservices.
codeExamples:
// Example Request Header
X-Trace-Id: 9f8d7a6b

expert.content:
Rate Limiting & Security

• Protect API from abuse by limiting requests.

Performance Optimization

• Improve request speed using:

  • • Caching
  • • Keep-Alive
  • • Compression (Gzip)
codeExamples:
// Enable Gzip in Spring Boot (application.properties)
server.compression.enabled=true

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Servlet view: the container turns the raw request into HttpServletRequest and gives you an empty HttpServletResponse to fill.
  • Parameters: getParameter reads query-string and form data; JSON bodies you must read yourself from getReader().
  • Committed response: once headers are sent you cannot change the status or redirect; this causes IllegalStateException.

Senior Notes

  • Threading: the container takes a thread from a pool for each request, so servlets must be thread-safe.
  • Keep-alive reuses a TCP connection for many requests, which saves handshake time.
  • Timeouts and buffering: the response is buffered (about 8 KB by default in many containers); flush explicitly for streaming.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Forward after commit: causes IllegalStateException; call return after redirect or forward.
  • Reading POST body twice: the stream can be read only once.
  • Encoding: set UTF-8 before reading parameters.
  • Duplicate form submit: use the post-redirect-get pattern.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance points:

  • Keep handlers short: a busy thread is not free for other requests.
  • Stream big responses instead of building them in memory.
  • Pool connections to the database.
  • Measure with access log time fields.
codeExamples:
<Valve className="org.apache.catalina.valves.AccessLogValve"
       directory="logs" prefix="access" suffix=".log"
       pattern="%h %m %U %s %b %D" />

// OUTPUT: (varies; %D is time in milliseconds)
// 127.0.0.1 GET /shop/products 200 5120 14

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a report page times out. Investigation:

  • Access log shows 30 second requests.
  • Thread dump shows threads waiting on the database.
  • Fix: add a query index, a timeout, and run the export asynchronously.

beginner.content:
What is a Web Server?

• A Web Server is a software that handles HTTP requests from clients (like browsers) and sends back responses (HTML, JSON, etc.).


What is Apache Tomcat?

  • • Open-source Java Servlet container
  • • Used to run Java web applications
  • • Supports Servlets and JSP

What is GlassFish?

  • • Full Java EE Application Server
  • • Supports Servlets, JSP, EJB, JPA, JMS
  • • More advanced than Tomcat

Tomcat vs GlassFish (Basic Difference)

  • • Tomcat → Lightweight, Servlet & JSP container
  • • GlassFish → Full Java EE server

How Web Server Works

  1. • Client sends HTTP request
  2. • Server processes request
  3. • Servlet handles logic
  4. • Response sent back to client

Fresher Notes

  • Web server serves static files over HTTP; an application server also runs Java code. Tomcat is a servlet container; GlassFish is a full Jakarta EE server.
  • Folders in Tomcat: bin (start scripts), conf (server.xml), webapps (apps) and logs.
  • Default port of Tomcat is 8080; the port is set in conf/server.xml on the Connector element.

Worked Example 1

Minimal web.xml and WAR layout.
codeExamples:
shop/
  index.jsp
  WEB-INF/
    web.xml
    classes/com/acme/HelloServlet.class
    lib/mysql-connector.jar

// OUTPUT:
// jar cvf shop.war -C shop .   ->  shop.war copied to webapps/ is served at /shop

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Tune the connector thread pool.
codeExamples:
<Connector port="8080" protocol="HTTP/1.1"
           maxThreads="200" minSpareThreads="10" acceptCount="100"
           connectionTimeout="20000" compression="on" />

// OUTPUT:
// up to 200 requests run at once; 100 more wait in the queue; the rest are refused

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Start and stop Tomcat on Windows and Linux.
codeExamples:
# Windows
bin\startup.bat
bin\shutdown.bat
# Linux
./bin/catalina.sh start
tail -f logs/catalina.out

// OUTPUT: (varies)
// INFO [main] org.apache.catalina.startup.Catalina.start Server startup in [820] milliseconds

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Change the HTTP port in server.xml.
codeExamples:
<Connector port="9090" protocol="HTTP/1.1"
           connectionTimeout="20000" redirectPort="8443" />

// OUTPUT:
// after restart: http://localhost:9090/ shows the Tomcat home page

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Tomcat is built from nested components.

  • Server and Service: the top of the tree.
  • Connector: protocol handling (HTTP, AJP), with a thread pool.
  • Engine, Host: virtual host routing.
  • Context: one web application with its own class loader.
  • Wrapper: one servlet.
  • Jasper: the JSP compiler.
codeExamples:
<Server port="8005" shutdown="SHUTDOWN">
  <Service name="Catalina">
    <Connector port="8080" protocol="HTTP/1.1" />
    <Engine name="Catalina" defaultHost="localhost">
      <Host name="localhost" appBase="webapps" autoDeploy="true" />
    </Engine>
  </Service>
</Server>

// OUTPUT:
// Server startup: webapps/shop.war is deployed as context /shop

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Deployment options:

  • WAR in webapps: easiest.
  • Context XML file: in conf/Catalina/localhost, to set a path or resources.
  • Manager app: upload or reload remotely.
  • Embedded Tomcat: a Java main starts the server (Spring Boot does this).
  • GlassFish: asadmin deploy shop.war.

intermediate.content:
Tomcat Architecture

  • • Connector → Handles HTTP requests
  • • Engine → Processes requests
  • • Host → Represents virtual host
  • • Context → Represents web application

Directory Structure (Tomcat)

  • • bin → Startup/Shutdown scripts
  • • conf → Configuration files
  • • webapps → Deploy applications here
  • • logs → Log files
codeExamples:
# Start Tomcat (Windows)
startup.bat

# Stop Tomcat
shutdown.bat

intermediate.content:
Deployment in Tomcat

• Applications are deployed as WAR (Web Archive) files.

Steps:

  1. • Create WAR file
  2. • Place inside webapps folder
  3. • Start server
  4. • Access using http://localhost:8080/appName
codeExamples:
<!-- web.xml example -->
<web-app>
  <servlet>
    <servlet-name>HelloServlet</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>com.example.HelloServlet</servlet-class>
  </servlet>

  <servlet-mapping>
    <servlet-name>HelloServlet</servlet-name>
    <url-pattern>/hello</url-pattern>
  </servlet-mapping>
</web-app>

intermediate.content:
GlassFish Features

  • • Admin Console (GUI)
  • • Supports EJB, JPA, JMS
  • • Clustering support
  • • Built-in security

expert.content:
Performance Tuning (Tomcat)

  • • Increase maxThreads in server.xml
  • • Configure connectionTimeout
  • • Enable compression
  • • Use connection pooling
codeExamples:
<!-- server.xml Connector configuration -->
<Connector port="8080"
           protocol="HTTP/1.1"
           maxThreads="200"

Servlet Lifecycle Deep Explanation

1. init()

• Called only once. Used for resource initialization like DB connection.


2. service()

• Handles multiple requests using multithreading. Not recommended to override directly in HttpServlet.


3. destroy()

• Used for cleanup activities like closing DB connections.

Multithreading in Servlet

• Servlet container creates one instance of servlet but multiple threads handle requests.

  • • Avoid instance variables
  • • Use local variables inside methods
  • • Ensure thread safety

Annotations vs web.xml

Feature Annotation web.xml
Configuration @WebServlet XML based
Ease of Use Easy More configuration
Modern Usage Recommended Legacy projects

  • • Servlet lifecycle methods order
  • • Difference between GenericServlet & HttpServlet
  • • Difference between ServletConfig & ServletContext
  • • Is Servlet thread-safe?
  • • How container manages servlet lifecycle?

Mid-Level Notes

  • One instance per servlet declaration; many threads call service() on it at the same time.
  • Mapping by @WebServlet("/path") or by web.xml; load-on-startup creates it at deploy time.
  • Config: ServletConfig gives init parameters of one servlet; ServletContext is shared by the whole app.

Senior Notes

  • Thread safety: do not keep per-request data in instance fields; use local variables and request attributes.
  • Cleanup: close pools and executors in destroy(), or better in a ServletContextListener.
  • Async: startAsync() frees the container thread during slow work such as remote calls.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

  • Instance fields for request data: use locals.
  • Heavy work in the constructor: use init.
  • Forgetting super.init(config): getServletConfig() returns null if you override init(ServletConfig).

  • Swallowing exceptions: log and return a proper status.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

  • Pool database connections.
  • Avoid synchronized on the whole service.

What is Loading?

• Loading means the servlet class is loaded into memory by the servlet container.


What is Instantiation?

Simple Flow

  1. • Class Loaded
  2. • Object Created
  3. • init() Called

Fresher Notes

  • Loading: the container finds the class from web.xml or @WebServlet, loads it and creates one instance with the no-argument constructor.
  • Lazy by default: without load-on-startup the servlet is created on the first request that maps to it.
  • Eager loading: <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup> or @WebServlet(loadOnStartup = 1) creates it when the application starts.

Worked Example 2

    <load-on-startup>2</load-on-startup>
</servlet>

// Servlet report is loaded after servlets with load-on-startup 0 or 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container (Catalina in Tomcat) turns a declaration into a ready servlet in a few steps.

  • Scan: at deployment it reads web.xml and scans classes for @WebServlet.
  • Wrapper: each declaration gets a wrapper object that holds the config, the mappings and the instance.
  • Load: the class is loaded by the web application classloader and created through reflection with the no-argument constructor.
  • Init: the container then calls init(ServletConfig) exactly once, and only after it succeeds can service() run.
  • Lazy path: without load-on-startup, the first request makes the wrapper allocate the servlet while later requests wait for that to finish.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to control loading:

  • Annotation: @WebServlet(loadOnStartup = n).
  • web.xml: <load-on-startup>n</load-on-startup>, and an empty element means any order.
  • Programmatic: ServletContext.addServlet() inside a ServletContainerInitializer or listener, then setLoadOnStartup().
  • Annotation or web.xml: web.xml settings override annotations for the same servlet name.
  • Metadata-complete: metadata-complete="true" turns annotation scanning off, which speeds startup.

intermediate.content:
Loading on First Request (Default Behavior)

• By default, servlet loads when the first request comes.


Loading at Server Startup

• Use load-on-startup in web.xml to load servlet during server startup.
codeExamples:
<!-- web.xml Configuration -->
<servlet>
  <servlet-name>DemoServlet</servlet-name>
  <servlet-class>com.example.DemoServlet</servlet-class>
  <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
</servlet>

<servlet-mapping>
  <servlet-name>DemoServlet</servlet-name>
  <url-pattern>/demo</url-pattern>
</servlet-mapping>

intermediate.content:
Annotation-Based Loading

• Modern way using @WebServlet annotation.

expert.content:
Deep Internal Working with Logging

• This example shows exact order of execution.

Expected Console Output Order

1. Class Loaded into Memory
2. Servlet Object Instantiated
3. init() method called
4. service() -> doGet() called
5. destroy() method called (when server stops)

Important Expert Notes

  • • Class loading happens only once per classloader.
  • • Only one servlet instance is created.
  • • Multiple requests are handled using multiple threads.
  • • Use loadOnStartup for heavy initialization tasks.

Interview Important Questions

Question Answer
When is a servlet class loaded and instantiated? By default on the first request; with load-on-startup (or loadOnStartup in @WebServlet) it happens at server startup instead
How many servlet objects does the container create? Only one instance per servlet class (per JVM) unless it implements the deprecated SingleThreadModel
What triggers class loading? Container classloader loads the .class file only once; static blocks run exactly once at that time
Constructor vs instantiation - same thing? Yes - the no-arg constructor runs at instantiation time, before init() is called

Mid-Level Notes

  • Order: a lower load-on-startup number loads first; a negative or missing value means lazy loading.
  • Constructor: keep it empty, because the ServletConfig and ServletContext are not available until init().
  • Packages: Tomcat 9 and older use javax.servlet.*; Tomcat 10+ and Jakarta EE 9+ use jakarta.servlet.*.

Senior Notes

  • Single instance: the container does not create one servlet per request or per user, so instance fields are shared by all threads.
  • Fail fast: load-on-startup makes configuration errors appear at deployment instead of at the first user request.
  • Several mappings: one servlet class declared twice in web.xml with different names gives two separate instances.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Missing public no-argument constructor: a constructor that needs arguments makes loading fail with InstantiationException; keep the default constructor.
  • Using getServletContext() in the constructor: it returns null or throws; move the code to init().
  • Assuming one instance per user: state is shared; keep user data in the session or request.
  • Wrong package for the container: javax.servlet classes on Tomcat 10+ are ignored or fail with ClassNotFoundException; switch to jakarta.servlet.
  • Duplicate mappings: two servlets with the same URL pattern fail deployment.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Load time can matter when the app has many servlets or heavy startup work.

  • Eager critical servlets: give load-on-startup to those that connect to databases or caches, so health checks see real readiness.
  • Lazy rare servlets: leave admin or report servlets lazy so startup stays short.
  • Scanning cost: exclude unused jars from annotation scanning (Tomcat jarsToSkip) and use metadata-complete for big apps.
  • Warm up: a load-on-startup servlet can also call its own heavy code paths once so the JIT is warm for the first user.
  • Measure: the container log timestamps show deploy time per app (varies).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

An online shop has a price-cache servlet that loads 50,000 products from the database. As a lazy servlet, the first customer after each deployment waited about 8 seconds (an example figure). The team set loadOnStartup = 1, so the load happens during deployment, and added a health check that waits for the cache. The load balancer now sends traffic only after the app is ready, and a database failure fails the deployment instead of hurting a customer.

What is init() Method?

• The init() method is a lifecycle method of a servlet.

  • • It is called only once.
  • • It is called when the servlet is first loaded.
  • • Used for initialization tasks.

Why We Use init()?

  • • Initialize database connection
  • • Load configuration file
  • • Initialize variables

Basic Example of init()

• This example shows init() method execution.

Fresher Notes

  • init() runs once after the instance is created and before any request is served.
  • Use it for one-time setup: read init parameters, open a data source lookup, load a properties file, warm a cache.
  • Two forms: init(ServletConfig config) and the no-argument init(); prefer the no-argument one in HttpServlet subclasses.

Worked Example 1

Looking up a DataSource once.

Worked Example 2

The config-based form.

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container calls init(ServletConfig) right after construction.

  • GenericServlet: stores the config in a field, then calls the no-argument init() hook, which is why overriding init() is easy and safe.
  • Visibility: the container publishes the initialized servlet safely, so fields set in init() are visible to request threads without extra locks.
  • Failure: a ServletException or RuntimeException makes the wrapper throw away the instance; UnavailableException adds a retry time (temporary) or none (permanent).
  • Requests meanwhile: a request for a servlet that is still initializing waits, or gets 503 if init failed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Where init data can come from:

  • Servlet init params: @WebInitParam or <init-param>, visible only to that servlet.
  • Context params: <context-param>, read with getServletContext().getInitParameter() by the whole app.
  • JNDI: data sources and environment entries.
  • Files: getServletContext().getResourceAsStream("/WEB-INF/app.properties").
  • System properties and env vars: for secrets and per-environment values.

Key Points

  • • Called only once per servlet lifecycle
  • • Executed before service()

expert.content:
Internal Working of init()

  1. • Servlet class is loaded
  2. • Servlet object created
  3. • Container calls init()
  4. • Servlet becomes ready to handle requests

Important:

• If init() fails, the servlet is marked as unavailable.

Real-World Example (Database Initialization)

Common expert-level use case: initialize DB connection pool in init().

Interview Important Points

  • • init() is called only once.
  • • Difference between init() and constructor?
  • • What happens if init() throws exception?
  • • Can we override both init() methods?
  • • When should heavy resources be initialized?

Constructor vs init()

Constructor init()
Called during object creation Called by container after object creation
No ServletConfig available ServletConfig available
Not recommended for heavy logic Best place for initialization logic

Mid-Level Notes

  • super.init(config): if you override the one-argument form you must call it, or getServletConfig() returns null.
  • Init parameters: read them with getInitParameter("name"); they come from @WebInitParam or <init-param>.
  • Exceptions: throw ServletException (or UnavailableException) when setup fails; the servlet is then not put into service.

Senior Notes

  • Failed init: the container may retry on the next request for a normal exception, so make init idempotent and clean up partial work.
  • Shared resources: build thread-safe objects here (a DataSource, an immutable config) and only read them in service().
  • Slow init: combine it with load-on-startup so the delay happens at deployment, not on a user request.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common init mistakes and fixes:

  • Forgot super.init(config): getServletConfig() and getInitParameter() then throw NullPointerException; override the no-argument init().
  • Swallowed exception: catching and only printing the error leaves a half-working servlet; rethrow as ServletException.
  • Parsing without a check: Integer.parseInt(null) fails with a poor message; validate and give a clear one.
  • Leaked resources on failure: if init opens a pool then fails, close it before throwing.
  • Mutable shared fields: filled in init but changed later by requests.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Init is the right place for expensive one-time work, but it should stay predictable.

  • Cache once: parse config, compile regular expressions and build immutable lookup maps here instead of per request.
  • Avoid long blocking: a slow remote call in init delays deployment; set timeouts.
  • Pool sizing: create the connection pool or thread pool here, sized from init params (varies by hardware).
  • Immutability: build immutable objects so request threads need no locks.
  • Lazy parts: use holder or lazy init for rarely used expensive objects.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A reporting servlet needs an API key, a template folder and a connection to a report database. In init() it reads the key from an environment variable, checks that the folder exists and tests the connection once. If anything is wrong it throws UnavailableException with a clear message, so the problem appears in the deployment log and monitoring marks the node unhealthy before users arrive.

beginner.content:
What is service() Method?

• The service() method is a lifecycle method of a servlet.

  • • It is called for every client request.
  • • It processes the request and sends response.
  • • After init(), service() handles all requests.

Simple Lifecycle Order

  1. • Servlet Loaded
  2. • init() called (once)
  3. • service() called (for every request)
  4. • destroy() called

Basic Example

• In HttpServlet, we usually override doGet() or doPost().

• Internally, service() calls doGet() or doPost().

Fresher Notes

  • service() is called by the container for every request, on a thread taken from the container pool.
  • HttpServlet.service() reads the HTTP method and calls doGet(), doPost(), doPut(), doDelete() and so on.
  • Normally you override doGet and doPost, not service() itself.

Worked Example 1

What dispatch looks like.

Worked Example 2

Thread name per request.

Practice Exercise 1

A shared field race.

Practice Exercise 2

Overriding service() carefully.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

For each request the container connector hands the work to a pool thread.

  • Request flow: connector parses the HTTP request, builds the request and response objects, runs the filter chain and finally calls servlet.service().
  • HttpServlet.service(ServletRequest, ServletResponse): casts to HTTP types and calls the protected service(HttpServletRequest, HttpServletResponse).
  • Dispatch: that method switches on the HTTP method name; for GET it also checks getLastModified() to support conditional GET (304).
  • Same instance: the same servlet object is used by all threads; only the request and response objects are new per request.
  • Recycling: request and response objects can be recycled, so never keep a reference after the method returns.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and related ideas:

  • Generic servlet: extend GenericServlet and implement service(ServletRequest, ServletResponse) for a non-HTTP protocol.
  • HEAD and OPTIONS: doHead reuses doGet without the body; doOptions lists the allowed methods.
  • Async: req.startAsync() frees the container thread while work continues elsewhere.
  • Multipart: @MultipartConfig enables getPart() for file upload.
  • Virtual threads: some containers can run each request on a virtual thread (Java 21+), but the shared-state rules stay the same.

intermediate.content:
How service() Works Internally

In HttpServlet:

  • • service() checks HTTP method (GET, POST, etc.)
  • • Calls respective method: doGet(), doPost(), etc.

Overriding service() Method

• We can override service() directly, but it is not recommended in HttpServlet.

GenericServlet service() Signature

public void service(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res)

In GenericServlet, we must override service().

expert.content:
Internal Flow of service() in HttpServlet

  1. • Client sends HTTP request
  2. • Container creates request & response objects
  3. • service() method is invoked
  4. • service() checks request.getMethod()
  5. • Calls doGet(), doPost(), etc.
  6. • Response sent back to client

Important: service() runs on multiple threads.

Threading Model

  • • Single servlet instance
  • • Multiple threads call service()
  • • Must avoid shared mutable instance variables

Best Practice

  • • Do not override service() in HttpServlet unless necessary
  • • Override doGet(), doPost(), etc.
  • • Use local variables inside methods

Interview Important Questions

  • • What is service() method?
  • • Difference between service() in GenericServlet and HttpServlet?
  • • Can we override service()?
  • • How does service() decide which method to call?
  • • Is service() thread-safe?

Tricky Question

Q: What happens if we override service() in HttpServlet?

A: doGet() and doPost() will NOT be called automatically unless explicitly invoked inside service().

Mid-Level Notes

  • Concurrency: many threads run service() on the same servlet object at the same time.
  • Safe data: local variables, request and response objects are per request; instance fields are shared.
  • Unsupported method: the default doGet() returns 405 or 400, so override only the methods you support.

Senior Notes

  • Thread safety: avoid mutable fields, or guard them with synchronized, atomics or concurrent collections.
  • Pool size: the container thread pool (for example maxThreads in Tomcat) limits how many requests run at once.
  • Overriding service(): do it only for cross-cutting needs and call super.service(); filters are usually a better place.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common service-time mistakes and fixes:

  • Mutable instance fields: for example a SimpleDateFormat or StringBuilder field; make it a local variable or use DateTimeFormatter.
  • Over-synchronizing: synchronized on the whole doGet turns the app into a single-user app; lock only small critical parts.
  • Keeping request or response in a field: later requests overwrite them.
  • Swallowing exceptions: the user gets an empty 200; let them propagate or send an error.
  • Writing the body twice: calling both getWriter() and getOutputStream() throws IllegalStateException.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance of service() is mostly about concurrency and what the thread does.

  • Do not block the pool: slow database or remote calls hold a thread; use timeouts, async or virtual threads.
  • Pool size: Tomcat maxThreads defaults to 200, and raising it without capacity only moves the queue.
  • Keep servlets thin: push business code into services that are easy to test and cache.
  • Avoid shared locks: prefer LongAdder or ConcurrentHashMap over synchronized counters.
  • Measure: use an access log valve or a metrics filter to track request time and thread use.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A checkout servlet had a field Order current that was set in doPost. In testing it worked, but under real traffic two customers sometimes saw each other's order summary. The fix was to make Order a local variable inside doPost and put the order id in the session. Load tests with many threads were added so the same race would be caught early.

beginner.content:
What is destroy() Method?

• The destroy() method is a lifecycle method of a servlet.

  • • It is called only once.
  • • Called before the servlet is removed from memory.
  • • Used for cleanup activities.

When is destroy() Called?

  • • When server is shutting down
  • • When servlet is reloaded
  • • When application is undeployed

Lifecycle Order

  1. • init() → called once
  2. • service() → called multiple times
  3. • destroy() → called once

Basic Example

• This example shows destroy() execution.

Fresher Notes

  • destroy() is called once when the container removes the servlet, for example at undeploy, reload or server shutdown.
  • Use it for cleanup: close connection pools, stop background threads, flush caches and release files.
  • After destroy() the instance is not used again and becomes eligible for garbage collection.

Worked Example 1

Lifecycle log of all three methods.

Worked Example 2

Shutdown wait.

Practice Exercise 1

Stopping a background task.

Practice Exercise 2

Independent closes.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container ends a servlet in a controlled order.

  • Trigger: undeploy, redeploy, context reload, or an orderly server stop (Tomcat shutdown script).
  • Quiesce: the container stops sending new requests to the servlet, and waits for running service() calls to end (the wait is limited).
  • Call: it then calls destroy() once and drops its reference, so the instance can be collected when nothing else points to it.
  • Order: servlets are destroyed in the reverse of loading order, and then context listeners get contextDestroyed (filters are destroyed before servlets in typical containers).
  • Exceptions: an exception thrown from destroy() is only logged; shutdown continues.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Cleanup choices:

  • destroy(): for resources owned by that servlet.
  • ServletContextListener: for app-wide resources such as a shared pool.
  • JVM shutdown hook: Runtime.addShutdownHook is risky in a container because it can leak the classloader.
  • AutoCloseable fields: keep them in a list and close in reverse order.
  • Graceful drain: stop accepting new work, finish running work, then close.

intermediate.content:
Why destroy() is Important?

• It is used to release resources created during init().


Common Cleanup Tasks

  • • Close database connection
  • • Close file streams
  • • Stop background threads
  • • Release memory resources
Real Example: Closing Database Connection

Important Notes

  • • destroy() is called only once.
  • • After destroy(), servlet becomes eligible for garbage collection.
  • • No new requests are processed after destroy() starts.

expert.content:
Internal Working of destroy()

  1. • Container stops accepting new requests.
  2. • Waits for current requests to complete.
  3. • Calls destroy() method.
  4. • Removes servlet instance from memory.

Important: destroy() runs in single thread by container.

Handling Long Running Tasks

• If servlet starts background threads, they must be stopped inside destroy().

Interview Important Questions

  • • When is destroy() called?
  • • Is destroy() called for every request?
  • • What happens if destroy() throws exception?
  • • Difference between finalize() and destroy()?
  • • Can destroy() be called multiple times?

destroy() vs finalize()


destroy() finalize()
Called by servlet container Called by Garbage Collector
Used for resource cleanup Used before object GC
Predictable execution Not guaranteed execution time

Mid-Level Notes

  • Waiting: the container tries to let running service() calls finish (or time out) before it calls destroy().
  • Not guaranteed: if the JVM is killed (kill -9, crash, power loss) destroy() never runs.
  • Symmetry: whatever init() opens, destroy() should close.

Senior Notes

  • Leaks: a thread started in init() and never stopped is the classic cause of redeploy memory leaks (ClassLoader leaks).
  • Robust cleanup: wrap each close in its own try-catch so one failure does not skip the rest.
  • Alternative: use ServletContextListener.contextDestroyed() for application-wide resources shared by many servlets.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Orphan threads: a non-daemon thread keeps running after undeploy; stop it in destroy() and give threads names for diagnosis.
  • JDBC driver leak: deregister drivers loaded by the app, or the old classloader stays in memory.
  • ThreadLocal values: clear them with remove(), or pooled container threads keep old objects.
  • Long destroy: a blocking wait with no timeout delays shutdown; use awaitTermination with a limit.
  • Relying on destroy for data safety: persist important data as you go.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cleanup speed affects redeploys and rolling restarts.

  • Bounded waits: use timeouts (for example 10 to 30 seconds, tune per app) so one stuck task does not block the node.
  • Fast flush: batch writes should flush quickly on shutdown.
  • Memory leaks: repeated redeploys in dev are a good test; watch heap and class counts with a profiler.
  • Container settings: Tomcat unloadDelay and stopTimeout control how long it waits.
  • Rolling restart: health endpoints should report "draining" so the load balancer stops traffic first.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

An email servlet queues messages in memory and sends them from a background worker. After a redeploy, queued mails were lost and the old worker thread kept running, so memory grew. The fix: destroy() stops accepting new mails, drains the queue to the database within a time limit, then stops the worker. The next instance reads pending mails at init().

beginner.content:
What is doGet()?

doGet() handles HTTP GET requests.

  • • Data is sent in URL
  • • Used for fetching data
  • • Data is visible in browser
  • • Limited data size

What is doPost()?

doPost() handles HTTP POST requests.

  • • Data is sent in request body
  • • Used for submitting form data
  • • Data is not visible in URL
  • • No size limitation (practically large)
Basic Example of doGet()
Basic Example of doPost()

Fresher Notes

  • doGet() handles HTTP GET: reading data, with parameters in the URL query string.
  • doPost() handles HTTP POST: submitting data, with parameters in the request body.
  • Signature: protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws ServletException, IOException.

Worked Example 1

Rejecting a missing parameter.

Worked Example 2

Unsupported method.

Practice Exercise 1

Reading both kinds of parameters.

Practice Exercise 2

Sharing one code path.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How a request reaches doGet or doPost:

  • Browser: a link, address bar or method="get" form sends GET; a form with method="post" sends POST.
  • Parsing: the container parses the query string for GET; for POST with application/x-www-form-urlencoded it parses the body on the first getParameter() call.
  • Dispatch: HttpServlet.service() picks the method by name; HEAD calls doGet and drops the body.
  • Body streams: if you read getInputStream() or getReader() first, parameters from the body are not parsed.
  • Limits: servers limit the URL length and POST size (Tomcat maxPostSize, default 2 MB for form data).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of request handling:

  • Other verbs: doPut, doDelete, doHead, doOptions for REST style APIs.
  • Forms: HTML forms only send GET and POST, so PUT and DELETE come from JavaScript.
  • JSON bodies: read the body with req.getReader() and parse it with a JSON library.
  • Multipart: add @MultipartConfig and use req.getPart("file").
  • Multi-value: getParameterValues() for checkboxes and getParameterMap() for all.

Difference Between doGet() and doPost()


Feature doGet() doPost()
Data Location URL Request Body
Security Less Secure More Secure
Data Size Limited Large
Usage Fetch Data Submit Data
Bookmarkable Yes No

<!-- GET Form -->
<form action="GetExample" method="get">

  <input type="submit">
</form>

<!-- POST Form -->
<form action="PostExample" method="post">
  Username: <input type="text" name="username">
  <input type="submit">
</form>

intermediate.content:
How service() Calls doGet() / doPost()

The service() method checks the HTTP method type:

  • • If method = GET → calls doGet()
  • • If method = POST → calls doPost()

expert.content:
Internal Flow

  1. • Client sends HTTP request
  2. • Container creates HttpServletRequest & HttpServletResponse
  3. • service() method invoked
  4. • Based on request.getMethod(), doGet() or doPost() executed

Handling Both GET and POST in Single Logic

Best practice: Call common method from both doGet() and doPost()

Security Best Practices

  • • Use POST for sensitive data (passwords)
  • • Use HTTPS for secure communication
  • • Validate all request parameters
  • • Prevent SQL Injection

Interview Important Questions

  • Difference between doGet() and doPost()?
  • Which is more secure?
  • Can doGet() call doPost()?
  • What happens if doPost() is not implemented?
  • Why POST is not bookmarkable?

Tricky Question

Q: If we type URL manually in browser, which method is called?

A: doGet() is called.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Idempotent: GET must not change server state, because browsers, caches and crawlers may repeat it; use POST for changes.
  • Visibility: GET data appears in the URL, history and logs, so never send passwords with GET.
  • Sharing logic: when both methods do the same job, let doPost call doGet (or a private method).

Senior Notes

  • Encoding: call req.setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8") before reading POST parameters, or non-ASCII text is garbled.
  • Post-Redirect-Get: after a successful POST send a redirect so a browser refresh does not submit the form twice.
  • Status codes: return 405 for unsupported methods, 400 for bad input and 201 for created resources instead of always 200.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Changing data in doGet: a crawler or prefetch can delete or create records; use POST.
  • Double submit: user presses refresh after POST; use Post-Redirect-Get and a token.
  • No encoding: garbled text from POST; call setCharacterEncoding first (or configure a filter).
  • Null parameters: getParameter returns null when missing, so check before use.
  • SQL built from parameters: use PreparedStatement to avoid SQL injection.
  • Output injection: escape user text before writing it in HTML to avoid XSS.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning request handling:

  • GET and caching: GET responses can be cached; set Cache-Control and ETag or override getLastModified.
  • Small handlers: parse, validate, call a service and write the result.
  • Stream big bodies: do not read huge uploads fully into memory.
  • Connection reuse: keep-alive is on by default; avoid blocking inside the handler.
  • Limit input: set maximum sizes and parameter counts (Tomcat maxParameterCount) against abuse.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A registration page uses doGet to show the empty form and doPost to process it. On success it saves the user and redirects to a welcome page (Post-Redirect-Get). On errors it forwards back to the form with messages in request attributes, so the visitor does not lose typed values.

beginner.content:
What is HttpServletResponse?

• HttpServletResponse is used to send data from server to browser.

  • • Sends text or HTML
  • • Used inside doGet() or doPost()
  • • Works with HttpServletRequest

Basic Example

• Sending simple text response:

Sending HTML Response

• Always set content type before sending HTML.

Fresher Notes

  • HttpServletResponse is the object you fill to send the reply: status line, headers and body.
  • Body: getWriter() for text, getOutputStream() for binary data; use only one of them per response.
  • Key calls: setContentType, setStatus, setHeader, sendRedirect and sendError.

Worked Example 1

JSON response.

Worked Example 2

File download.

Practice Exercise 1

Plain text, status and headers.

Practice Exercise 2

Redirect and error.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The response object wraps a buffered output channel.

  • Parts: status line, headers, then the body, written in that order on the wire.
  • Buffer: the body goes first to a buffer (commonly 8 KB); headers stay changeable until the buffer is flushed or full.
  • Commit: the first flush sends status and headers, so after that setStatus, setHeader and sendRedirect have no effect or throw.
  • Writer or stream: getWriter() encodes characters with the response charset; getOutputStream() sends raw bytes.
  • Completion: when the servlet returns, the container flushes, closes the response and, with keep-alive, reuses the connection.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Most used response features:

  • Status: setStatus(int) for normal codes; sendError(code, msg) to use the container error page.
  • Redirect: sendRedirect(url) (302); for 301 or 303 set the status and the Location header yourself.
  • Headers: setHeader replaces, addHeader adds; date and int variants exist.
  • Cookies: addCookie(cookie) with setHttpOnly, setSecure and setMaxAge.
  • Content: setContentType, setCharacterEncoding, setContentLength.
  • URL rewriting: encodeURL adds the session id when cookies are off.

intermediate.content:
Setting Content Type

• Content type tells browser what type of data is being sent.

  • • text/html → HTML page
  • • text/plain → Normal text
  • • application/json → JSON data
  • • application/xml → XML data
codeExamples:
response.setContentType("application/json");
response.getWriter().write("{\"status\":\"success\"}");

intermediate.content:
sendRedirect()

• Redirects the browser to another page.

  • • URL changes
  • • New request is created
  • • Client-side redirection
codeExamples: response.sendRedirect("login.jsp");

intermediate.content:
Setting Status Codes

• We can send HTTP status codes manually.
codeExamples:
response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_OK);        // 200
response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_NOT_FOUND); // 404

intermediate.content:
Adding Cookies

• Used for session tracking.

expert.content:
Response Buffering & Commit (Advanced)

  • • Response is first stored in buffer
  • • When buffer is full → response is committed
  • • After commit → cannot redirect or forward

• Committed response means headers are already sent to client.

Forward vs Redirect (Deep Comparison)

Feature forward() sendRedirect()
Execution Server-side Client-side
URL Change No Yes
Performance Faster Slightly slower
Request Scope Same request New request

Sending File Download (Advanced)

• Used to download files from server.

Sending JSON API Response

• Used in REST APIs.

Advanced Methods

  • • setHeader() vs addHeader()
  • • setCharacterEncoding()
  • • setContentLength()
  • • encodeURL()
  • • sendError()
codeExamples:
response.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_FORBIDDEN,
                   "Access Denied");

expert.content:
Interview Advanced Questions

  • • What is response commit?
  • • Difference between getWriter() and getOutputStream()?
  • • When to use sendError()?
  • • Can we call sendRedirect() after writing response?
  • • Difference between setHeader() and addHeader()?

Mid-Level Notes

  • Order matters: set status, headers and content type before writing the body, because after the response is committed they are ignored.
  • Committed: the response is committed once the buffer is flushed; isCommitted() tells you, and a later sendRedirect throws IllegalStateException.
  • Redirect: sendRedirect sends a 302 and the browser makes a new request; a forward stays inside the server.

Senior Notes

  • Character set: resp.setContentType("text/html;charset=UTF-8") must be set before getWriter().
  • Buffering: tune setBufferSize, and call flushBuffer() for streaming such as large downloads.
  • Security headers: add X-Content-Type-Options, cache control and cookie flags (HttpOnly, Secure) centrally in a filter.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Headers after writing: status and headers set after the buffer flush are lost; set them first.
  • Redirect after output: IllegalStateException: Cannot call sendRedirect() after the response has been committed; redirect before writing and return.
  • Both writer and stream: getWriter() then getOutputStream() throws IllegalStateException.
  • Missing return after sendRedirect: the code continues and tries to write more.
  • Wrong content type: HTML sent as text/plain shows as raw text.
  • No charset: accented characters show as question marks.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Response tuning:

  • Compression: enable gzip in the connector for text content (Tomcat compression="on") instead of coding it.
  • Cache headers: static content gets long max-age, dynamic data no-store where needed.
  • Streaming: for large files copy in chunks (for example 8 to 64 KB) and avoid building whole content in memory.
  • Content-Length: set it for known sizes to avoid chunked encoding.
  • Slow clients: use async writes or timeouts so they do not pin threads.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A bank statement servlet must send a PDF, make sure it is never cached, and show a friendly error when the account is unknown. It sets the status and headers first, validates input before writing any bytes, and uses sendError for failures. A filter adds security headers to every response, so each servlet stays small.

beginner.content:
What is HttpServletRequest?

• HttpServletRequest is used to receive data from client (browser) to server.

  • • Gets form data
  • • Gets URL parameters
  • • Gets request headers
  • • Works inside doGet() and doPost()

Getting Form Data

• Use getParameter() to read input values.

Getting Multiple Values

• Used for checkbox or multi-select inputs.

Fresher Notes

  • Request object: the container builds one HttpServletRequest per HTTP request and passes it to doGet or doPost.
  • What it holds: method, URL, headers, parameters, cookies, session and the body stream.
  • Common getters: getMethod(), getRequestURI(), getHeader("User-Agent"), getRemoteAddr().

Worked Example 1

URL parts.

Worked Example 2

Attribute for a forward.

Practice Exercise 1

Print basic request info.

Practice Exercise 2

List all header names.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container parses the raw HTTP message and wraps it in a request object.

  • Connector: reads the request line and headers from the socket, then builds the object (in Tomcat a Request wrapped by a facade).
  • Lazy parsing: the body and parameters are parsed on the first call to getParameter or getReader.
  • Pooling: the objects are recycled after the response, which is why you must not keep a reference.
  • Interfaces: ServletRequest is protocol neutral; HttpServletRequest adds headers, cookies and session.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful groups of methods:

  • Line: getMethod, getRequestURI, getProtocol, getScheme.
  • Headers: getHeader, getHeaders, getIntHeader, getDateHeader.
  • Body: getReader, getInputStream, getContentLength.
  • Client: getRemoteAddr, getLocale, getCookies.
  • State: getSession(false), attributes.
  • Imports: Jakarta EE 9+ uses jakarta.servlet.http.*; Java EE and Tomcat 9 use javax.servlet.http.*.

intermediate.content:
Request Methods

  • • GET → Data visible in URL
  • • POST → Data sent in body
  • • PUT, DELETE → Used in REST APIs
codeExamples:
String method = request.getMethod();
System.out.println("Request Type: " + method);

intermediate.content:
Getting Request Headers

• Headers contain browser and request information.
Getting Client Information

Request Attributes

• Used to pass data between servlets (forward).

expert.content:
Request Lifecycle (Advanced)

  1. • Client sends HTTP request
  2. • Container creates HttpServletRequest object
  3. • Servlet processes request
  4. • Response sent back
  5. • Request object destroyed

getParameter() vs getAttribute()

Feature getParameter() getAttribute()
Data Source Client form data Server-side data
Data Type String Object
Used In Form processing Forward/include

Reading Raw Data (Advanced)

• Used when receiving JSON data in REST APIs.

File Upload (Multipart Request)

• Requires @MultipartConfig annotation.

Advanced Methods

  • • getRequestURI()
  • • getRequestURL()
  • • getContextPath()
  • • getSession()
  • • getCookies()
  • • getInputStream()

Interview Advanced Questions

  • 1. Difference between GET and POST?
  • 2. Difference between getParameter() and getAttribute()?
  • 3. How to read JSON from request?
  • 4. What is multipart request?
  • 5. How does request lifecycle work?

Mid-Level Notes

  • Parameters or attributes: parameters come from the client and are always Strings; attributes are server-side objects you set with setAttribute.
  • URL parts: getContextPath(), getServletPath() and getPathInfo() together make up getRequestURI().
  • Body is read once: after getParameter reads a form body, getReader() may return nothing.

Senior Notes

  • Never trust it: headers such as X-Forwarded-For and Host can be forged, so validate or take them only from a trusted proxy.
  • Wrappers: HttpServletRequestWrapper lets a filter change headers, parameters or the body for later servlets.
  • Not thread safe: never store the request in a field or pass it to another thread after the service method returns.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • getCookies null: the array is null, not empty, when no cookie exists.
  • getSession() creates: it makes a session for every visitor; use getSession(false) to only look.
  • Reading the body twice: a filter that reads the body leaves nothing for the servlet; wrap and cache it.
  • Trusting headers: Referer and X-Forwarded-For are client controlled.
  • Keeping the request: using it in another thread after return gives wrong or recycled data.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Request handling is cheap, but a few habits help:

  • Avoid sessions for anonymous traffic, since each one uses memory.
  • Stream large bodies with getInputStream instead of reading them into a String.
  • Limits: configure maxPostSize, header size and connection timeouts in the connector.
  • Async: startAsync() frees the container thread while a slow backend call runs.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A logging filter records each request, using a wrapper for the real client address.

  • Proxy: trust X-Forwarded-For only from your own load balancer.
  • Privacy: do not log passwords, tokens or full query strings that hold secrets.
  • Correlation id: read or create a request id and put it in the log context.

beginner.content:
What is text/html Response?

text/html tells the browser that the response contains HTML content.

  • • Used to display web pages
  • • Must set content type before writing output
  • • Uses PrintWriter

Fresher Notes

  • Writer: resp.getWriter() gives a PrintWriter for text; the HTML you print becomes the response body.
  • Set type first: call setContentType("text/html;charset=UTF-8") before getWriter().
  • One body: use either getWriter() or getOutputStream() for a response, not both.

Worked Example 1

Escaping user input.

Worked Example 2

Check committed state.

Hello page.

A small table.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The response is built in a buffer and sent when committed.

  • Buffer: default size is usually 8 KB (getBufferSize()); small pages are sent in one go with a Content-Length.
  • Commit: the status line and headers are written on the first flush or when the buffer fills.
  • Writer: PrintWriter encodes characters with the response charset.
  • PrintWriter swallows IOException: check checkError() if you care.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to produce a body:

  • getWriter(): text and HTML.
  • getOutputStream(): binary data such as images.
  • forward to a JSP: the usual choice for pages.
  • setBufferSize / resetBuffer / reset: control and clear the buffer before commit.
  • sendError(404): produce the container error page.

intermediate.content:
Complete HTML Page Generation

  • • Dynamic content from database
  • • Display form data
  • • Conditional rendering

Character Encoding Importance

  • • Prevents special character issues
  • • Supports UTF-8 languages
  • • Must be set before writing output
codeExamples: response.setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8");

intermediate.content:
Setting Content Length

• Improves performance by telling browser response size.

Auto-Flushing & Closing Stream

  • • Container auto flushes buffer
  • • Manual close not always required
  • • Flushing commits response
codeExamples:

out.flush();  // commits response

Response Buffer Internals

  • • Default buffer size (usually 8KB)
  • • Can change using setBufferSize()
  • • Once committed → headers locked
codeExamples:
response.setBufferSize(16384); // 16KB
int size = response.getBufferSize();

expert.content:
Checking Commit Status

• Used to avoid IllegalStateException.

Mixing getWriter() & getOutputStream()

• You cannot use both in same response.

• If used together → IllegalStateException.

Performance Considerations

  • • Avoid heavy HTML generation in Servlet
  • • Use JSP/Thymeleaf for view layer
  • • Follow MVC pattern
  • • Minimize string concatenation

Security Considerations

  • • Prevent XSS by escaping user input
  • • Validate request parameters
  • • Avoid exposing sensitive data
codeExamples:
String user = request.getParameter("user");
// Escape HTML before printing

expert.content:
Real-World Flow

  1. • Client sends request
  2. • Servlet processes business logic
  3. • Generates dynamic HTML
  4. • Response buffered
  5. • Committed to client

Advanced Interview Questions

  • 1. What happens if content type is not set?
  • 2. Explain response buffering mechanism.
  • 3. What is response commit?
  • 4. Difference between flush() and close()?
  • 5. Can we reset response after commit?
  • 6. Why MVC is recommended instead of writing HTML in servlet?

Mid-Level Notes

  • Escape output: user data printed into HTML must be encoded (< becomes <) or you create an XSS hole.
  • Buffering: output is buffered; flush() sends the status line and headers, after which they cannot change.
  • HTML in Java strings is hard to maintain, so use a JSP or a template for real pages and keep servlets for logic.

Senior Notes

  • Status first: set status and headers before the first byte is committed; check isCommitted().
  • Streaming: for big pages flush in chunks (chunked transfer encoding) instead of building a huge String.
  • Security headers: add Content-Security-Policy and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff to HTML responses.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • XSS: printing request data raw; encode it for HTML.
  • Type after writer: setting charset after getWriter() has no effect.
  • Both writer and stream: throws IllegalStateException.
  • Hand-built HTML: hard to read and test; use JSP, JSTL c:out or a template engine.
  • Missing html escape in attributes: quotes inside value="..." break out of the attribute.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Compression: enable gzip on the connector or in a filter for HTML.
  • Buffer size: a larger buffer lets you change status or redirect later, but uses more memory per request.
  • Streaming: flush periodically for long reports so the user sees progress.
  • StringBuilder: build big strings with it, or write directly to the writer.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A health page for a load balancer.

  • Cheap: no database call, or a very fast one.
  • No cache: add Cache-Control: no-store.
  • Status: return 503 when the app is not ready so the balancer stops sending traffic.

beginner.content:
What is Content Type?

• Content-Type tells the browser what type of data the server is sending.

  • • text/html → HTML page
  • • text/plain → Normal text
  • • application/json → JSON data
  • • application/pdf → PDF file

• We use response.setContentType() to set it.

Fresher Notes

  • Content-Type header tells the browser how to read the body, set with resp.setContentType("text/html").
  • Common types: text/html, text/plain, application/json, application/pdf, image/png.
  • Charset: add it as text/html;charset=UTF-8 so non-English text shows correctly.

Worked Example 1

File download.

Worked Example 2

Choose type from Accept.

Practice Exercise 1

Plain text versus HTML.

Practice Exercise 2

JSON response.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The content type is just a header plus a hint to the writer.

  • Header: setContentType writes Content-Type; a charset part also sets the character encoding.
  • Order: the writer fixes its encoding when first obtained, so set the type first.
  • Container default: if no charset is given, the servlet default is ISO-8859-1 (Servlet 4 and earlier); newer containers can set a default in web.xml or response-character-encoding.
  • Case: header names are case insensitive; types are conventionally lower case.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Typical values:

  • Text: text/html, text/plain, text/css, text/csv.
  • Data: application/json, application/xml.
  • Files: application/pdf, application/zip, application/octet-stream.
  • Images: image/png, image/jpeg.
  • Guess it: getServletContext().getMimeType("a.png") uses the container mime mappings.

intermediate.content:
Common Content Types

Type Used For
text/html Web Pages
text/plain Simple Text
application/json REST API
application/xml XML Data
image/png Images

Sending JSON Response

• Used in REST APIs.

Setting Character Encoding

• Prevents special character issues.

What Happens if Not Set?

  • • Browser may treat data as plain text
  • • File download may not work properly
  • • JSON may display incorrectly

expert.content:
Internal Working of Content-Type

  • • Content-Type is an HTTP response header
  • • Sent before response body
  • • Browser decides how to render content

Example HTTP Response:

• HTTP/1.1 200 OK 
• Content-Type: text/html;charset=UTF-8

Buffer & Commit Rule

  • • Content type must be set before response is committed
  • • After commit → headers cannot be changed

Difference: setContentType() vs setHeader()

Method Purpose
setContentType() Sets Content-Type header safely
setHeader("Content-Type", ...) Manual header setting

File Download Example

• Proper content type required for file download.

Security Considerations

  • • Always set correct content type to prevent MIME sniffing
  • • Use X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header
codeExamples: response.setHeader("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff");

expert.content:
Advanced Interview Questions

  • 1. Why must content type be set before writing response?
  • 2. What happens if content type is not set?
  • 3. Difference between setContentType and setHeader?
  • 4. Explain MIME types.
  • 5. Can we change content type after response commit?

Mid-Level Notes

  • Wrong type: HTML sent as text/plain shows tags as text; JSON sent as HTML is risky for XSS.
  • setCharacterEncoding on the response must be called before getWriter(); the request one is a different method for the input.
  • Downloads: add Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="report.pdf" to force a Save dialog.

Senior Notes

  • nosniff: send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff so browsers do not guess a different type from the content.
  • Default: with no type set, the container may send none or a default; always set it explicitly.
  • Content negotiation: choose the type from the Accept header, and set Vary: Accept for caches.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • No charset: accented text shows as garbage; add ;charset=UTF-8.
  • JSON as text/html: clients may not parse it, and it invites XSS.
  • Setting after commit: ignored once the response is committed.
  • Uploads served as HTML: user files must be served with a safe type, nosniff and a download disposition.
  • Binary through the writer: corrupts bytes; use the output stream.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance related:

  • Content-Length: lets the client reuse the connection and show progress.
  • Caching: static types need Cache-Control and ETag.
  • Compression: compress text types only; images and zips are already compressed.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

One endpoint serving both browsers and API clients.

  • Negotiate using Accept.
  • Errors should use the same type the client asked for.
  • Security headers on every response through a filter.

beginner.content:
What is sendRedirect()?

sendRedirect() is used to redirect the browser to another URL.

  • • URL changes in browser
  • • New request is created
  • • Client-side redirection
  • • Uses HTTP status code
  • • Request data is not preserved

Basic Example

Redirect user to login page:
