  • • Used inside doGet() or doPost()
  • • Does NOT stop execution - the method returns normally and code after it still runs, so add an explicit return;
  • • Browser sends new request

Fresher Notes

  • sendRedirect tells the browser to make a new request: resp.sendRedirect("home.jsp") sends status 302 with a Location header.
  • Browser does it: the URL in the address bar changes, and the browser sends a second GET.
  • Request data lost: request attributes and parameters are not carried to the new request.

Worked Example 1

Safe redirect target.

Worked Example 2

Post-Redirect-Get.

Practice Exercise 1

Simple redirect.

Practice Exercise 2

Redirect after login.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A redirect is only a response; the browser does the work.

  • Server side: sendRedirect sets status 302, writes the Location header, clears the buffer and commits the response.
  • Relative paths: resolved by the container against the request URL; a leading / is relative to the server root, not the context, so add getContextPath().
  • Client side: the browser sends a new GET to the Location URL (cookies for that host are sent).
  • Code after it still runs: add return.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Choices:

  • 302 Found: the default temporary redirect.
  • 301 Moved Permanently: cached by browsers; set status and header yourself.
  • 303 See Other: redirect after POST using GET.
  • 307 / 308: keep the original method and body.
  • encodeRedirectURL: adds a session id when cookies are off.

intermediate.content:
How sendRedirect Works

  • • Server sends HTTP status 302
  • • Location header contains new URL
  • • Browser receives new URL
  • • Browser sends completely new request
  • • Previous request object destroyed

Flow:

  1. • Client → Servlet
  2. • Servlet → 302 Response
  3. • Browser → New Request

Redirect to External Website

  • • Can redirect outside application
  • • Useful for third-party login
  • • Works with full URL
codeExamples: response.sendRedirect("https://www.google.com");

intermediate.content:
Redirect with Parameters

  • • Parameters passed in URL
  • • Data visible in browser
  • • Suitable for small data only
codeExamples:
String name = "Ashish";
response.sendRedirect("welcome.jsp?user=" + name);

intermediate.content:
Common Use Cases

  • • After successful login
  • • After form submission (PRG Pattern)
  • • Redirect HTTP to HTTPS
  • • Unauthorized access redirect
  • • Logout redirection

expert.content:
HTTP Status Code Behind sendRedirect()

sendRedirect() internally sends:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /newURL
  • • 302 → Temporary redirect
  • • Location header contains new URL
  • • Browser automatically follows redirect
  • • SEO impact depends on status code

Redirect vs Forward (Deep Comparison)

Feature sendRedirect() forward()
Type Client-side Server-side
URL Changes Yes No
New Request Yes No
Request Scope Data Lost Available

  • • Redirect is slower than forward
  • • Redirect can go outside application
  • • Forward works only inside server

Response Commit Rule

  • • sendRedirect() must be called before response is committed
  • • If response already written → IllegalStateException
  • • Buffer size affects commit
  • • Cannot write response after redirect

Post/Redirect/Get (PRG Pattern)

Prevents duplicate form submission.

  • • Client submits form (POST)
  • • Server processes data
  • • Server redirects to GET page
  • • Prevents refresh duplicate submission

Permanent Redirect (301)

Manually setting status for SEO-friendly redirect:

  • • 301 → Permanent redirect
  • • Search engines update URL
  • • Better for SEO migration
codeExamples:
response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_MOVED_PERMANENTLY);
response.setHeader("Location", "https://example.com");

expert.content:
Advanced Interview Questions

  • • Difference between sendRedirect and forward?
  • • Which HTTP status code is used in redirect?
  • • Why is PRG pattern important?
  • • Can we redirect after writing response?
  • • How to perform permanent redirect?
  • • Why redirect is slower than forward?

Mid-Level Notes

  • Redirect or forward: redirect is a round trip to the client and can leave the application; forward stays on the server.
  • Post-Redirect-Get: redirect after a successful POST so a page refresh does not submit the form again.
  • Carry data across a redirect with the session, a flash attribute or query parameters; encode with URLEncoder.

Senior Notes

  • Open redirect: never redirect to a raw next parameter; allow only relative paths or a whitelist of hosts.
  • Cannot redirect after commit: once the response is committed, sendRedirect throws IllegalStateException.
  • Status codes: use setStatus(303) plus a Location header when you need 303 or 307 instead of the default 302.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Open redirect: using an unchecked parameter as the target enables phishing.
  • Forgetting return: the code continues and may write a body or redirect twice.
  • Redirect after output: throws IllegalStateException.
  • Expecting attributes: request attributes are gone; use the session or the URL.
  • Unencoded parameters: spaces and ampersands break the query string.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cost and tuning:

  • Extra round trip: a redirect adds one request, so avoid chains of redirects.
  • Prefer forward inside the application when the URL need not change.
  • 301 caching: a permanent redirect saves repeated trips, but a mistake is hard to undo in browsers.
  • Link directly to the final URL in pages you control.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Login flow with a safe return URL.

  • Remember the requested page in the session or a validated parameter.
  • Validate the return path as local.
  • PRG: redirect after the POST so the back button is safe.

beginner.content:
What is RequestDispatcher?

RequestDispatcher is used to forward request from one resource to another resource inside the server.

  • • Server-side redirection
  • • URL does NOT change
  • • Same request & response object used
  • • Works inside same application
  • • Faster than sendRedirect()

forward() Method

Transfers control to another resource (Servlet/JSP/HTML).

  • • Stops current servlet execution
  • • Control fully transferred
  • • Browser unaware of forwarding
  • • Same request object shared

include() Method

Includes output of another resource in current response.

  • • Includes resource output
  • • Current servlet continues execution
  • • Used for header/footer
  • • Output appended to response

Fresher Notes

  • RequestDispatcher passes a request to another servlet or JSP on the server: req.getRequestDispatcher("result.jsp").
  • forward: hands control to the target, which produces the whole response; the browser URL does not change.
  • include: adds the output of another resource into the current response, then continues.

Worked Example 1

Validate then forward or redirect.

Worked Example 2

Dispatcher by name.

Practice Exercise 1

Forward with data.

Practice Exercise 2

Include a header.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Dispatching happens fully inside the container.

  • Lookup: the container maps the path to a servlet or JSP through the same rules as a normal request.
  • Forward: clears the unflushed buffer, runs the target, then closes the response.
  • Include: the target cannot change the status or headers; such calls are ignored.
  • Attributes: the container sets jakarta.servlet.forward.request_uri (or javax.servlet.forward.*) so the target can see the original URL.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Where to get a dispatcher:

  • request.getRequestDispatcher(path): path may be relative to the current resource.
  • context.getRequestDispatcher(path): path must start with /.
  • context.getNamedDispatcher(name): by servlet name.
  • Query string: the path may contain one, such as /view.jsp?mode=edit.
  • Cross context: context.getContext("/other") then its dispatcher, if allowed.

intermediate.content:
How forward() Works

  • • Stops current servlet execution
  • • Transfers request internally
  • • Browser is unaware
  • • Request attributes remain available
  • • Uses same request & response object

Passing Data using Request Scope

  • • request.setAttribute()
  • • request.getAttribute()
  • • Data available in same request
  • • Commonly used between Servlet → JSP

include() Behavior

  • • Includes output of another resource
  • • Main servlet continues execution
  • • Useful for header/footer
  • • Response content appended

Example: include() Full Flow

  • • Write main content
  • • Include another resource
  • • Continue writing response

forward() vs include()

Feature forward() include()
Stops current execution Yes No
URL changes No No
Output control Transferred Appended

expert.content:
Internal Working

  • • Container creates RequestDispatcher object
  • • Control transferred within same request
  • • No new HTTP request generated
  • • Uses same thread
  • • Faster than sendRedirect()
  • • Works only inside same application

Response Commit Rule

  • • forward() must be called before response is committed
  • • If response already committed → IllegalStateException
  • • Cannot redirect after forward()
  • • Buffer size matters

Common MVC Pattern Usage

Servlet acts as Controller.

  • • Servlet processes data
  • • Sets request attributes
  • • Forwards to JSP (View)
  • • Model contains business logic

Common Mistakes

  • • Writing response before forward()
  • • Using forward() after redirect()
  • • Expecting URL change
  • • Forwarding to external website

Interview Important Questions

  • • Difference between forward() and include()?
  • • Difference between forward() and sendRedirect()?
  • • Can we forward to external website?
  • • Does forward create new request?
  • • Why is forward faster than redirect?

Tricky Question

Q: Can we forward to another server?

A: No. forward() works only inside same application/server.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Same request: forward and include share the same request and response, so setAttribute data is visible to the target.
  • Path rules: a path starting with / is relative to the context root; no slash means relative to the current servlet.
  • No output before forward: the response buffer must not be committed, or forward throws IllegalStateException.

Senior Notes

  • WEB-INF: JSPs placed under /WEB-INF/ cannot be opened directly, so forwarding is the only way in (a good MVC rule).
  • Dispatcher types: filters can be mapped to FORWARD, INCLUDE, ERROR and ASYNC dispatches, not only REQUEST.
  • Return after forward: code after forward() still runs, so return to avoid writing twice.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Output before forward: flushed content causes IllegalStateException.
  • No return: code after forward runs and may forward or redirect again.
  • Forward then refresh on POST: the browser URL is the POST, so a refresh resubmits; use redirect for success.
  • Dispatcher null: a path the container cannot map may give null, so check.
  • User-controlled path: forwarding to req.getParameter("page") exposes internal files such as WEB-INF.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance:

  • Cheap: a forward has no network round trip, so it is faster than a redirect.
  • Include for fragments is fine, but a deep chain of includes adds overhead; prefer JSP tags or templates.
  • Avoid heavy attributes: keep large objects out of the request unless the view needs them.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Front controller (MVC) pattern.

  • One servlet receives all *.do or /app/* requests.
  • Action runs the logic and stores a model in the request.
  • View is chosen by name and forwarded from /WEB-INF.

beginner.content:
What is getParameter()?

getParameter() is used to read form data sent from client to server.

  • • Reads form input values
  • • Returns data as String
  • • Works with GET and POST
  • • Defined in HttpServletRequest

HTML Form Example

  • • Form sends data to servlet
  • • Input name attribute is important
codeExamples:
<form action="login" method="post">
  Name: <input type="text" name="username" />
  <input type="submit" value="Submit" />
</form>

beginner.content:
Reading Form Data in Servlet

  • • Use request.getParameter("fieldName")
  • • Always returns String

Fresher Notes

  • getParameter: req.getParameter("name") returns the value of an input field as a String, or null if it is missing.
  • Name match: the argument must equal the name attribute of the HTML input, not its id.
  • Same call for GET (query string) and POST (body) data.

Worked Example 1

Safe number parsing.

Worked Example 2

All parameters.

Practice Exercise 1

Read two fields.

Practice Exercise 2

Checkboxes.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Form data is parsed by the container from the query string and the body.

  • GET: parameters come from the query string, application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
  • POST: the same encoding in the body, parsed on the first getParameter call.
  • Decoding: percent encoding is decoded using the request encoding (body) or the connector URIEncoding (query, UTF-8 by default in Tomcat 8+).
  • Multipart: multipart/form-data bodies are parsed only with @MultipartConfig.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Reading options:

  • getParameter: one value.
  • getParameterValues: all values.
  • getParameterNames: enumeration of names.
  • getParameterMap: read-only map of all.
  • getPart: files and multipart fields.
  • JSON body: use getReader() and a JSON library, because getParameter does not parse JSON.

intermediate.content:
Handling Multiple Form Fields

  • • Read multiple parameters
  • • Validate input
  • • Convert String to int/double

Handling Checkbox & Multiple Values

  • • Use getParameterValues()
  • • Returns String array
  • • Used for checkbox/multi-select

GET vs POST Data Reading

  • • GET → Data visible in URL
  • • POST → Data sent in request body
  • • getParameter() works for both

Handling Null Values

  • • Parameter may return null
  • • Always check before using

expert.content:
Character Encoding Handling

  • • Important for non-English characters
  • • Must set encoding before reading parameters
  • • Prevents garbage characters
codeExamples:
request.setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8");

String name = request.getParameter("username");

expert.content:
Reading All Parameters Dynamically

  • • Use getParameterMap()
  • • Use getParameterNames()
  • • Useful for dynamic forms

Security Considerations

  • • Never trust client input
  • • Validate all parameters
  • • Prevent SQL Injection
  • • Prevent XSS attacks

Common Mistakes

  • • Forgetting input name attribute
  • • Not handling null values
  • • Not setting character encoding
  • • Parsing without validation

Advanced Interview Questions

  • • Difference between getParameter() and getAttribute()?
  • • What does getParameterValues() return?
  • • Why does getParameter() always return String?
  • • How to handle UTF-8 form data?
  • • How to prevent form data security issues?

Mid-Level Notes

  • Multiple values: use getParameterValues("hobby") for checkboxes and multi-selects; it returns a String[] or null.
  • Convert and check: numbers arrive as Strings, so use Integer.parseInt inside try-catch for NumberFormatException.
  • Encoding: call req.setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8") before the first getParameter on a POST.

Senior Notes

  • Validate on the server: client checks are only a convenience; check null, length, range and format again.
  • Parameter pollution: ?id=1&id=2 gives two values, and getParameter returns only the first.
  • Limits: containers cap the number and size of parameters (for example Tomcat maxParameterCount, maxPostSize) against denial of service.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Null not checked: getParameter("age").trim() throws NullPointerException.
  • Wrong name: using the id attribute instead of name.
  • Garbled UTF-8: forgetting setCharacterEncoding, or calling it after a parameter was read.
  • Unchecked boxes: an unchecked checkbox sends nothing, so null means false.
  • Concatenated SQL: leads to SQL injection.
  • Printing raw: leads to XSS.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and limits:

  • Parameter count: a huge number of parameters is a denial of service vector, so keep the connector maxParameterCount reasonable (Tomcat default 10000).
  • POST size: maxPostSize limits the body parsed as parameters (Tomcat default 2 MB).
  • Large uploads: set maxFileSize, maxRequestSize and fileSizeThreshold.
  • Parse once: store the converted object in a request attribute instead of re-parsing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A registration form handler combining the good practices.

  • Encoding first.
  • Validate each field and collect errors.
  • Forward back with errors and old values (escaped in the JSP) or redirect on success.

beginner.content:
What is GET Method?

  • • Used to fetch data
  • • Data sent in URL
  • • Visible in browser address bar
  • • Limited data size
  • • Not secure for sensitive data

What is POST Method?

  • • Used to send data to server
  • • Data sent in request body
  • • Not visible in URL
  • • More secure than GET
  • • No size limitation (practically large)
Basic Servlet Example

Fresher Notes

  • GET reads data: parameters travel in the URL query string, so the request can be bookmarked and cached.
  • POST sends data in the request body, so it suits forms that change data, such as login or checkout.
  • Servlet methods: override doGet and doPost; service() dispatches by HTTP method.

Worked Example 1

Post/Redirect/Get.

Worked Example 2

Rejecting an unsupported method.

Practice Exercise 1

A servlet that handles both methods.

Practice Exercise 2

Reading the query string on GET.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container turns each HTTP request into an HttpServletRequest and calls service().

  • Dispatch: HttpServlet.service reads the method and calls doGet, doPost, doPut and so on.
  • GET data: the query string is parsed lazily when you first call getParameter.
  • POST data: for application/x-www-form-urlencoded the container reads the body and merges it with the query parameters.
  • HEAD and OPTIONS: HEAD reuses doGet without the body; OPTIONS lists the overridden methods.
  • Multipart: file uploads need @MultipartConfig and getPart().

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax and variants:

  • Form: method="get" is the default; enctype may be urlencoded, multipart or text/plain.
  • Annotations: @WebServlet("/x") maps the URL; both methods share one class.
  • Other verbs: HTML forms only send GET and POST; PUT and DELETE come from fetch or AJAX.
  • Parameters: getParameterValues for multi-value, getParameterMap for all.
  • Body: JSON bodies are read with getReader(), not getParameter.

intermediate.content:
GET vs POST Comparison

Feature GET POST
Data Location URL Request Body
Security Less Secure More Secure
Data Length Limited Large
Bookmarkable Yes No

HTML Form Example

  • • method="get"
  • • method="post"
codeExamples:
<!-- GET Example -->
<form action="user" method="get">
  Name: <input type="text" name="username" />
  <input type="submit" />
</form>

<!-- POST Example -->
<form action="user" method="post">
  Name: <input type="text" name="username" />
  <input type="submit" />
</form>

intermediate.content:
Reading Parameters (Same for Both)

  • • request.getParameter()
  • • Works for GET & POST
  • • Always returns String
codeExamples:
String name = request.getParameter("username");
response.getWriter().println("Hello " + name);

intermediate.content:
When to Use GET

  • • Searching data
  • • Filtering records
  • • Idempotent operations
  • • Read-only requests

When to Use POST

  • • Login forms
  • • Registration forms
  • • File upload
  • • Database insert/update

expert.content:
HTTP Internals

  • • GET appends query string to URL
  • • POST sends data in request body
  • • GET is idempotent
  • • POST is not idempotent
  • • GET can be cached
  • • POST usually not cached

Security Considerations

  • • GET parameters logged in browser history
  • • GET visible in server logs
  • • POST still not encrypted unless HTTPS
  • • Always use HTTPS for sensitive data

Redirect Behavior

  • • After POST → Use PRG (Post/Redirect/Get)
  • • Prevents duplicate submission
  • • Browser refresh resubmits POST

Handling Both in One Method

  • • Call doPost() inside doGet()
  • • Or override service()
  • • Avoid duplicate logic

Advanced Interview Questions

  • • Difference between GET and POST?
  • • Which method is idempotent?
  • • Why POST is not fully secure?
  • • Can GET modify server data?
  • • What is PRG pattern?
  • • Why GET can be cached?

Mid-Level Notes

  • Safe and idempotent: GET must not change server state; repeating a PUT or DELETE gives the same result, a POST may not.
  • Post/Redirect/Get: after a successful POST, call response.sendRedirect() so a browser refresh does not resubmit the form.
  • Encoding: call request.setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8") before reading POST parameters, otherwise non-ASCII text is garbled.

Senior Notes

  • Never put secrets in GET: URLs end up in browser history, proxy logs and the Referer header.
  • CSRF: POST alone is not protection; add a per-session token and check SameSite cookies.
  • Limits: servers cap URL and header size (often 8 KB), while the POST body limit is set by the container, for example maxPostSize in Tomcat.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong encoding: read parameters before setCharacterEncoding, so text is garbled; set it first or use a filter.
  • Sensitive data in GET: passwords end up in logs; switch to POST over HTTPS.
  • State change on GET: a link like /delete?id=3 can be triggered by crawlers or image tags.
  • No redirect after POST: refresh resubmits the order.
  • Forgetting doPost: the form returns 405.
  • Parsing numbers without checking: NumberFormatException gives a 500; validate and return 400.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Caching: GET responses can carry Cache-Control and ETag; POST is not cached.
  • Body limits: set maxPostSize and upload limits to stop abuse.
  • Streaming: read large bodies as streams, not as one string.
  • Parameter count: Tomcat caps maxParameterCount to resist hash-collision attacks.
  • Compression: enable gzip for text responses at the connector or a filter.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a product search page and a checkout form.

  • Search: GET, so results are bookmarkable and cacheable.
  • Checkout: POST with a CSRF token, then redirect to a confirmation page.
  • Idempotency key: a hidden unique id lets the server ignore a double click.

beginner.content:
What are Hidden Fields?

Hidden fields are form input elements that are not visible to users but send data to the server.

  • • Used to store hidden data
  • • Data sent with form submission
  • • Used for session tracking
  • • Visible in page source (not secure)

HTML Hidden Field Example

  • • type="hidden"
  • • Has name and value
  • • Not displayed in browser
codeExamples:
<form action="profile" method="post">
  <input type="hidden" name="userId" value="101" />
  Name: <input type="text" name="username" />
  <input type="submit" value="Submit" />
</form>

beginner.content:
Reading Hidden Field in Servlet

  • • Use request.getParameter()
  • • Works like normal form field

Fresher Notes

  • Hidden field: <input type="hidden" name="step" value="2"> carries data with a form but shows nothing on screen.
  • State on a stateless protocol: the value comes back to the servlet on submit, so you can pass data between pages of a form.
  • Reading it: use request.getParameter("step"), exactly like a visible field.

Worked Example 1

CSRF token in a hidden field.

Worked Example 2

Tampered price.

Practice Exercise 1

Carrying a record id in an edit form.
codeExamples:
<form action="update" method="post">
  <input type="hidden" name="id" value="42">
  <input name="name" value="Abaji">
  <button>Save</button>
</form>

// OUTPUT:
// POST /update  body: id=42&name=Abaji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Reading it in the servlet.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A hidden field is ordinary form data with no visible control.

  • Browser: it serializes every named control, hidden or not, into the query string or body on submit.
  • Server: the container cannot tell it from a visible field; both appear in getParameterMap.
  • No storage: the value lives only in the page HTML; a new page load needs the servlet to write it again.
  • Trust: the data crosses the user machine twice, so treat it as user input.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Plain value: ids, steps, return URLs.
  • Token: CSRF or one-time form key.
  • Signed value: add an HMAC so tampering is detectable.
  • JSP output: use <c:out> or fn:escapeXml to encode the value.
  • Alternative: keep the state in HttpSession and send only a step id.

intermediate.content:
Hidden Fields for Session Tracking

  • • Used when cookies disabled
  • • Data passed between pages
  • • Requires form submission
  • • Maintains user state

Passing Hidden Field to Next Page

  • • Servlet generates dynamic hidden value
  • • Embedded inside form

Hidden Fields vs Cookies

Feature Hidden Field Cookie
Stored Where? Inside Form Browser
Requires Form Submit? Yes No
Security Less Secure Moderate

expert.content:
Security Considerations

  • • User can modify hidden field value
  • • Never trust hidden field data
  • • Always validate on server side
  • • Not suitable for sensitive data

Hidden Fields Limitation

  • • Works only with forms
  • • Not suitable for large data
  • • Cannot persist across direct URL access
  • • Not ideal for complex session handling

Real World Use Cases

  • • Multi-step form data passing
  • • CSRF token storage
  • • Temporary state management
  • • E-commerce cart step tracking

Hidden Field vs URL Rewriting vs HttpSession

Feature Hidden Field URL Rewriting HttpSession
Visible to User No (but viewable in source) Yes (URL) No
Security Low Low High
Best Use Form Data Passing Small Session Tracking Full Session Management

Advanced Interview Questions

  • • What is hidden field in servlet?
  • • How hidden field maintains session?
  • • Why hidden field is not secure?
  • • Difference between hidden field and cookie?
  • • When should you avoid hidden fields?

Mid-Level Notes

  • Not secret: anyone can see and edit a hidden field with View Source or developer tools.
  • Always revalidate: re-check price, role and ids on the server; never trust the hidden value.
  • Multi-step forms: copy earlier answers into hidden fields, or store them in the session and keep only a step id in the page.

Senior Notes

  • Tampering: a hidden price field is a classic vulnerability; look the price up in the database instead.
  • CSRF token: a hidden random token stored also in the session proves the form came from your site.
  • Escape output: when you write a value back into value="...", HTML-escape it to avoid XSS.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Trusting price or role: look them up server-side.
  • Unescaped values: a quote in the value breaks the HTML and enables XSS.
  • Leaking secrets: API keys or passwords in hidden fields.
  • Stale data: two browser tabs overwrite each other; add a version field and check it.
  • Missing name attribute: a field without name is not submitted.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Page weight: every hidden field is sent on each submit, so a wizard that copies big data bloats requests.
  • Prefer the session for large or many values.
  • ViewState-style frameworks compress and sign such state; do the same if you carry much.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: an edit-profile page.

  • Hidden id identifies the record, checked against the logged-in user.
  • Hidden CSRF token blocks forged submits.
  • Hidden version detects concurrent edits.

beginner.content:
What is URL Rewriting?

URL Rewriting is a session tracking technique where data is appended to the URL as query parameters.

  • • Data is added at the end of URL
  • • Format: ?key=value
  • • Multiple values separated using &
  • • Used when cookies are disabled

Basic Example

  • • Passing username through URL
  • • Data visible in browser address bar
codeExamples: response.sendRedirect("welcome.jsp?user=Ashish");

beginner.content:
Reading URL Data in Servlet

  • • Use request.getParameter()
  • • Works like form data

Fresher Notes

  • URL rewriting adds data to the link itself, for example /cart?item=7 or /cart;jsessionid=ABC123.
  • Works without cookies: it is the fallback when the browser blocks cookies.
  • Servlet API: response.encodeURL(url) adds the session id only when needed.

Worked Example 1

Redirect with a session id.

Worked Example 2

Cookie-only tracking in web.xml.
codeExamples:
<session-config>
  <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode>
</session-config>

// OUTPUT:
// URLs are never rewritten, encodeURL(x) returns x unchanged

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Encoding a link.

Practice Exercise 2

Query parameter with safe encoding.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container decides in encodeURL whether rewriting is needed.

  • Check: it adds the id when the session is new, or the request did not arrive with a cookie.
  • Format: a path parameter ;jsessionid=ID is added before the query string.
  • Incoming: the container parses the path parameter and finds the session.
  • Absolute URLs to other hosts are never rewritten, which protects the id from leaking to them.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • encodeURL: for links, form actions and images.
  • encodeRedirectURL: for sendRedirect.
  • Query parameters: your own data, not the session, such as ?page=2.
  • Path parameters: ;key=value matrix style.
  • Tracking modes: COOKIE, URL, SSL (set in web.xml or on the context).

intermediate.content:
Multiple Parameters Example

  • • Separate parameters using &
  • • Format: ?key1=value1&key2=value2
codeExamples: response.sendRedirect("profile?name=Ashish&role=admin");

intermediate.content:
URL Rewriting for Session Tracking

  • • Session ID added in URL
  • • Useful when cookies disabled
  • • Maintains user state
codeExamples:
String sessionId = "12345";
response.sendRedirect(response.encodeRedirectURL("dashboard"));  // appends ;jsessionid=... which is the ONLY form the container parses; a sessionId query param does NOT reattach the session

intermediate.content:
Encoding URL Properly

  • • Use encodeURL()
  • • Automatically appends session ID if needed
codeExamples:
String url = response.encodeURL("home.jsp");
response.sendRedirect(url);

intermediate.content:
URL Rewriting vs Hidden Fields

Feature URL Rewriting Hidden Field
Data Visible Yes No (but viewable in source)
Works Without Form Yes No
Security Low Low

expert.content:
How Container Uses URL Rewriting

  • • When cookies disabled, container appends session ID
  • • Format: ;jsessionid=XXXX
  • • Automatically handled by encodeURL()

Example:

http://localhost:8080/app/home;jsessionid=ABC123

encodeURL() vs encodeRedirectURL()

  • • encodeURL() → for normal links
  • • encodeRedirectURL() → for sendRedirect()

Security Considerations

  • • Data visible in browser
  • • Can be bookmarked
  • • Can be modified by user
  • • Not safe for sensitive data

Limitations

  • • URL length limitation
  • • Not suitable for large data
  • • Manual handling required for every link
  • • Less secure than HttpSession

URL Rewriting vs HttpSession vs Cookies

Feature URL Rewriting Cookies HttpSession
Security Low Medium High
Visible to User Yes No No
Best Use When Cookies Disabled Light Tracking Full Session Management

Advanced Interview Questions

  • • What is URL rewriting in servlet?
  • • How does encodeURL() work?
  • • What happens when cookies are disabled?
  • • Difference between encodeURL() and encodeRedirectURL()?
  • • Why is URL rewriting not secure?
  • • What is ;jsessionid in URL?

Mid-Level Notes

  • encodeRedirectURL: use it for sendRedirect, because redirects follow different rules than normal links.
  • Every link must be encoded; one forgotten link loses the session.
  • Query string data is visible, bookmarkable and length-limited, so keep it small and not secret.

Senior Notes

  • Leak risk: a session id in the URL appears in logs, history and the Referer header, which enables session hijacking.
  • Disable it: in Servlet 3.0+ set <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode> in web.xml so ids are never put in URLs.
  • Encode parameters with URLEncoder.encode(value, UTF_8) so spaces and symbols do not break the URL.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Not encoding a link: that page loses the session when cookies are off.
  • Encoding twice: do not wrap an already encoded URL.
  • Hand-built jsessionid: never append it yourself.
  • Query strings with raw text: unencoded & or spaces break parsing.
  • Logging full URLs: they contain the id; strip it in access logs.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cost: encodeURL is cheap, but URLs vary per user so shared caches cannot reuse the pages.
  • CDN: pages with jsessionid in links defeat caching; switch to cookie tracking.
  • Tomcat: the disableURLRewriting context attribute turns it off in Tomcat 8.5+ (check your version).
codeExamples:
<!-- META-INF/context.xml (Tomcat) -->
<Context path="/shop" cookies="true" />
<!-- web.xml -->
<session-config><tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode></session-config>

// OUTPUT:
// links stay identical for all users, so CDN and browser caches work

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: an older intranet app must still work on kiosks with cookies blocked.

  • Keep rewriting but only over HTTPS and on an internal network.
  • Short timeout reduces the window for a leaked id.
  • Bind the session to a client attribute where practical and rotate the id after login.

beginner.content:
What is a Cookie?

• A cookie is a small piece of data stored in the user's browser by the server.
• It helps maintain state in web applications (since HTTP is stateless).


Why Cookies are Needed?

  • • Maintain login sessions
  • • Store user preferences (theme, language)
  • • Track user activity
  • • Personalization
  • • Shopping cart management

Real-Life Example

• When you log in to an e-commerce website, the server stores a session cookie.
• That cookie tells the server who you are on every request.


How Cookies Work

  1. • User sends request to server
  2. • Server responds with Set-Cookie header
  3. • Browser stores the cookie
  4. • Browser sends cookie automatically in future requests

Client-Side vs Server-Side Cookies

  • • Client-side → Created using JavaScript
  • • Server-side → Created using backend (Spring Boot, Node, etc.)
codeExamples:
// Creating Cookie using JavaScript
document.cookie = "username=Ashish; expires=Fri, 31 Dec 2026 12:00:00 UTC; path=/";

// Reading Cookies
console.log(document.cookie);

// Deleting Cookie
document.cookie = "username=; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 UTC; path=/";

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Cookie: a small name-value pair the server sends in Set-Cookie and the browser returns in every matching request.
  • Servlet API: new Cookie(name, value), response.addCookie(c) and request.getCookies().
  • Lifetime: setMaxAge(seconds); without it the cookie is a session cookie and dies when the browser closes.

Worked Example 1

Helper that finds a cookie.

Worked Example 2

SameSite through a header.

Practice Exercise 1

Set and read a cookie.

Practice Exercise 2

Delete a cookie.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Cookies are plain HTTP headers.

  • Set: the response carries Set-Cookie: name=value; attributes.
  • Send: the browser stores it and adds Cookie: name=value to every request matching domain, path and Secure rules.
  • Container: addCookie only formats the header; getCookies parses the Cookie header.
  • Expiry: Max-Age is a countdown, Expires a date; browsers prefer Max-Age.
  • Order: a cookie is chosen by the most specific path first.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Attributes and variants:

  • Max-Age / Expires: persistent versus session cookie.
  • Path / Domain: scope; a Domain makes the cookie available to subdomains.
  • HttpOnly / Secure: script protection and HTTPS only.
  • SameSite: Strict, Lax or None (None requires Secure).
  • Cookie prefixes: __Host- forces Secure, Path=/ and no Domain.
  • Servlet 6: setAttribute("SameSite", "Lax") exists on Cookie.

intermediate.content:
Types of Cookies

  • • Session Cookies - Deleted when browser closes
  • • Persistent Cookies - Stored until expiry date
  • • Secure Cookies - Sent only over HTTPS
  • • HttpOnly Cookies - Not accessible via JavaScript
  • • SameSite Cookies - Protect against CSRF attacks

Cookie Attributes

  • • Expires / Max-Age
  • • Domain
  • • Path
  • • Secure
  • • HttpOnly
  • • SameSite

When to Use Cookies vs Session

  • • Use Session for temporary authentication
  • • Use Persistent Cookie for "Remember Me"

Server-Side Cookie (Spring Boot Example)

expert.content:
Security Considerations

  • • XSS Protection - Use HttpOnly flag
  • • CSRF Protection - Use SameSite=Strict or Lax
  • • HTTPS Enforcement - Use Secure flag

SameSite Modes

  • • Strict - Cookie sent only for same-site requests
  • • Lax - Sent for top-level navigation
  • • None - Sent for all requests (requires Secure)

JWT vs Cookies

• JWT can be stored inside cookies or localStorage.
• Storing JWT in HttpOnly cookie is more secure than localStorage
• because it prevents JavaScript access (reduces XSS risk).


Cookie Size & Limitations

  • • 4KB per cookie
  • • 20-50 cookies per domain (browser dependent)
  • • Sent with every HTTP request (affects performance)

Advanced Concepts

  • • Signed Cookies (prevent tampering)
  • • Encrypted Cookies
  • • Token Rotation Strategy
  • • Refresh Token stored in HttpOnly cookie

Best Practices

  • • Store minimal data
  • • Always use HttpOnly + Secure in production
  • • Set proper expiration
  • • Avoid storing sensitive data directly
  • • Rotate tokens periodically
codeExamples:
// Example Set-Cookie Header
Set-Cookie: token=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/; Max-Age=3600

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Scope: setPath and setDomain decide which URLs receive the cookie.
  • Delete a cookie by sending the same name, path and domain with setMaxAge(0).
  • getCookies() can be null when the request has no cookies, so check before the loop.

Senior Notes

  • HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript and limits XSS damage; Secure sends it only over HTTPS.
  • SameSite (Lax or Strict) limits cross-site sending and helps against CSRF; set it with a header or container config.
  • No sensitive data: store an opaque id in the cookie and the data on the server; the client can edit any cookie.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Delete fails: path or domain differs from the original; repeat them exactly.
  • Spaces or semicolons in the value: encode with URLEncoder or Base64.
  • NullPointerException: check getCookies() for null.
  • Setting a cookie after the response is committed: headers must be added before writing the body.
  • Storing passwords or roles: store an opaque id server-side.
  • Missing Secure on HTTPS sites: the cookie can leak over HTTP.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Size: cookies are sent with every request, including images; keep them small.
  • Static domain: serve static files from a cookie-free domain or path.
  • Count: fewer, shorter cookies lower header cost; limits are about 4 KB each (varies).
  • Lifetime: short for authentication, longer for preferences.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: a remember-me login.

  • Selector and validator: store a random token pair, only a hash of the validator in the database.
  • Rotate the token on each use and delete it at logout.
  • Flags: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, and a limited life such as 30 days.

beginner.content:
What is HttpSession?

• HttpSession is an interface provided by Java Servlet API that allows you to store user-specific data on the server side.

• Since HTTP is stateless, HttpSession helps maintain user state across multiple requests.


Why HttpSession is Needed?

  • • Maintain user login state
  • • Store user-specific data (username, role)
  • • Shopping cart management
  • • Temporary server-side storage

How HttpSession Works

  1. • User sends first request
  2. • Server creates session and generates Session ID
  3. • Session ID is stored in JSESSIONID cookie
  4. • Browser sends JSESSIONID in future requests
  5. • Server retrieves session using Session ID

Important Point

• Session data is stored on the server, not in the browser.
codeExamples:
// Creating / Getting Session
HttpSession session = request.getSession();

// Storing Data in Session
session.setAttribute("username", "Ashish");

// Getting Data from Session
String username = (String) session.getAttribute("username");

// Removing Attribute
session.removeAttribute("username");

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • HttpSession keeps per-user data on the server between requests; get it with request.getSession().
  • Session id: the container sends a JSESSIONID cookie, and the browser returns it to find the session.
  • Attributes: setAttribute, getAttribute and removeAttribute; end the session with invalidate().

Worked Example 1

Visit counter per user.

Worked Example 2

Secure cookie config in web.xml.
codeExamples:
<session-config>
  <session-timeout>20</session-timeout>
  <cookie-config>
    <http-only>true</http-only>
    <secure>true</secure>
  </cookie-config>
  <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode>
</session-config>

// OUTPUT:
// Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=...; Path=/shop; Secure; HttpOnly

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Login and read back.

Practice Exercise 2

Logout.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Session data stays in server memory; the client holds only an id.

  • Creation: getSession() makes a StandardSession in a map keyed by id (Tomcat) and sends Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID.
  • Lookup: each request id is looked up and lastAccessedTime updated.
  • Expiry: a background thread removes sessions idle longer than the max inactive interval.
  • Persistence: Tomcat can save sessions on restart (PersistentManager) if attributes are serializable.
  • Listeners: HttpSessionListener and HttpSessionAttributeListener observe changes.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

API variants:

  • getSession(true/false): create or only find.
  • changeSessionId(): new id, same data (Servlet 3.1+).
  • invalidate(): destroy now.
  • setMaxInactiveInterval(n): seconds; a negative value means never expire (avoid it).
  • Binding listener: HttpSessionBindingListener on an attribute reacts to bind and unbind.
  • Package: jakarta.servlet.http in Tomcat 10+, javax.servlet.http in Tomcat 9.

intermediate.content:
Session Lifecycle

  • • Session is created using request.getSession()
  • • Session remains active until timeout or invalidation
  • • Default timeout: 30 minutes (configurable)

Configuring Session Timeout (web.xml)

< session-config >
  < session-timeout >15< /session-timeout  >
< /session-config >

Invalidate Session (Logout)

• When user logs out, session should be invalidated.


Difference: getSession(true) vs getSession(false)

  • • true → creates new session if not exists
  • • false → returns null if session not exists
codeExamples:
// Set Session Timeout (Programmatically)
session.setMaxInactiveInterval(10 * 60); // 10 minutes

expert.content:
Session Tracking Mechanisms

  • • Cookies (JSESSIONID)
  • • URL Rewriting
  • • Hidden Form Fields
  • • SSL Sessions

Session Fixation Attack

• An attacker sets a known session ID before login.
• After login, attacker reuses the same session.


Prevention

  • • Invalidate old session after login
  • • Create new session ID

Session vs Cookies

  • • Session → Stored on server
  • • Cookies → Stored on browser
  • • Session more secure for sensitive data

Best Practices

  • • Always invalidate session on logout
  • • Set proper timeout
  • • Do not store large objects in session
  • • Use HTTPS
codeExamples:
// URL Rewriting Example
response.encodeURL("dashboard.jsp");

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • getSession(false) returns null instead of creating a new session; use it to check whether a user is logged in.
  • Timeout: set in web.xml with <session-timeout>30</session-timeout> (minutes) or setMaxInactiveInterval(seconds).
  • Logout: call invalidate(), and the old id stops working.

Senior Notes

  • Session fixation: call request.changeSessionId() right after login so an attacker-chosen id is replaced.
  • Memory and clustering: keep sessions small and attributes Serializable; use sticky sessions or a shared store such as Redis.
  • Cookie flags: configure HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite through <cookie-config>.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • No fixation defense: call changeSessionId() after login.
  • Using getSession() to test login: it creates sessions for bots; use getSession(false).
  • Non-serializable attributes: replication and restart fail.
  • Mutating a stored object without setAttribute: clustered stores do not notice; call setAttribute again.
  • Thread safety: sessions are shared across tabs; synchronize changes to mutable objects.
  • Huge attributes: large lists exhaust memory.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Memory: sessions times average size is your heap cost; store ids, not objects.
  • Timeout: shorter timeouts free memory; 15 to 30 minutes is common.
  • Bots: avoid creating sessions for anonymous pages.
  • Clustering: sticky sessions are cheapest; replication costs network; Redis is common.
  • JSP: add <%@ page session="false" %> where no session is needed.
codeExamples:
<%@ page session="false" %>
<!-- public page: no JSESSIONID created -->

// OUTPUT:
// response has no Set-Cookie header, no session object allocated

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: login with a shopping cart.

  • Before login: anonymous cart in the session.
  • On login: rotate the id, merge the cart, set a user attribute.
  • Idle timeout: 20 minutes, with a warning for a longer absolute limit.
  • Logout: invalidate and expire the cookie.

beginner.content:
What is URL Rewriting?

• URL Rewriting is a session tracking technique where session data (usually a session ID) is appended to the URL.

• It is commonly used when cookies are disabled in the browser.


Example URL:

http://example.com/home;jsessionid=12345


Why Use URL Rewriting?

  • • Maintains session without cookies
  • • Simple to implement
  • • Works in all browsers

Fresher Notes

  • Compare the options: cookies are simple and automatic, sessions keep data on the server, URL rewriting works when cookies are off.
  • Default: the container tries a cookie first and rewrites URLs only until it knows cookies work.
  • jsessionid in a path, as in /app/page;jsessionid=..., is the sign that rewriting is active.

Worked Example 1

Forcing cookie-only mode in code.

Worked Example 2

Stateless link with a signed token.

Practice Exercise 1

Using c:url in a JSP.
codeExamples: <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %> Orders // OUTPUT: (varies) // first response: Orders // after cookie: Orders

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Checking how the session is tracked.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

This topic is about choosing a tracking technique, not the mechanics of one link.

  • Cookie: data on the client, sent automatically; the session id usually rides in one.
  • Session: data on the server, referenced by that id.
  • URL rewriting: the same id carried in the path when cookies fail.
  • Hidden field: data carried only through form posts.
  • Container logic: the first response includes both a cookie and a rewritten URL; once a cookie returns, rewriting stops.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Comparison to guide the choice:

  • Cookies: small, per-browser preferences; need user consent in many regions.
  • HttpSession: login state, carts; needs server memory.
  • URL rewriting: only when cookies are unavailable; least secure.
  • Hidden fields: multi-page forms.
  • Query parameters: shareable state such as search filters and page numbers.
  • Token in header: APIs and mobile clients.

intermediate.content:
How URL Rewriting Works Internally

• When a client makes a request, the server creates a session and generates a unique session ID.

• If cookies are disabled, the server appends the session ID to the URL.


Methods Used in Servlet API:

  • • response.encodeURL(String url)
  • • response.encodeRedirectURL(String url)

Advantages

  • • Does not depend on cookies
  • • Easy session tracking

Disadvantages

  • • Session ID visible in URL
  • • Security risks (URL sharing)
  • • URL length increases

expert.content:
Security Considerations in URL Rewriting

• Since the session ID is visible in the URL, it can be exposed via:

  • • Browser history
  • • Bookmarks
  • • Log files
  • • Referer headers

Security Risks

  • • Session Hijacking
  • • Session Fixation

Best Practices

  • • Always use HTTPS
  • • Regenerate session ID after login
  • • Use encodeURL() instead of manual appending
  • • Prefer cookies when available

When to Use URL Rewriting?

• URL Rewriting should be used only when cookies are disabled or not supported. Modern applications prefer cookies or token-based authentication.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Choose by need: preferences go in a cookie, user state in the session, shareable or stateless links in query parameters.
  • JSP: <c:url value="/cart"/> calls encodeURL for you, so prefer it over hard-coded links.
  • Bookmarks: a link with a session id, once bookmarked, is stale or dangerous; never share such links.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer cookie tracking in modern apps; rewriting widens the attack surface through logs and Referer leaks.
  • REST and APIs avoid sessions: use tokens in the Authorization header instead of URL ids.
  • Search engines may index jsessionid URLs and create duplicate pages; disabling rewriting avoids it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes when mixing techniques:

  • Sharing a link with jsessionid: the other person joins your session.
  • Relying on rewriting for security: it does not add any.
  • Redirects without encodeRedirectURL in cookie-less clients.
  • Cookie and URL ids disagreeing: the container prefers the cookie; clear stale URLs.
  • Third-party cookie blocking: embedded widgets lose cookies even if your site works; test it.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Caching: cookie tracking keeps URLs identical, so CDNs and browsers cache pages.
  • SEO: no jsessionid duplicates.
  • Stateless alternatives remove session memory and sticky-session needs.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world scenario: pick the tracking for three features of one shop.

  • Language preference: cookie, lives 6 months.
  • Cart and login: session with cookie-only tracking, fixation defense.
  • Product filters: query parameters, so links can be shared and cached.

beginner.content:
What are Hidden Form Fields?

• Hidden Form Fields are a session tracking technique where data is stored inside an HTML form using input fields of type hidden.

• The data is not visible to the user but is sent to the server when the form is submitted.


Why Use Hidden Fields?

  • • Maintain user data between requests
  • • Simple implementation
  • • Works without cookies
codeExamples:
<!-- HTML Example -->
<form action="nextServlet" method="post">
    <input type="hidden" name="username" value="Ashish" />
    <input type="submit" value="Next" />
</form>

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Hidden field: <input type="hidden" name="step" value="2"> is sent with the form but not shown on screen.
  • Stateless trick: HTTP forgets each request, so a hidden field carries a small value (step number, item id) from one page to the next.
  • Not secret: the user can see it with View Source or change it with browser tools, so never trust it blindly.

Worked Example 1

Tampering demo.
codeExamples:
<input type="hidden" name="price" value="500">
<!-- the user edits value to 1 in the browser tools and submits -->

// OUTPUT:
// The server receives price=1. Fix: ignore it and load the price by product id.

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

CSRF token in a hidden field.

Practice Exercise 1

Wizard step 1 passing data to step 2.
codeExamples:
<form action="step2" method="post">
  Name: <input type="text" name="name">
  <input type="hidden" name="step" value="1">
  <input type="submit" value="Next">
</form>

// OUTPUT:
// POST /step2  body: name=Abaji&step=1  (the step value is never shown on the page)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Servlet echoing the hidden value into the next form.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A hidden field is plain form data with no visual control.

  • Encoding: the browser adds it to the query string (GET) or the body (POST) like any other input.
  • Server view: the container parses it into getParameter with no difference from a visible field.
  • Trust: the value is client input, so the same validation applies as for a text box.
codeExamples:
<form method="post" action="checkout">
  <input type="hidden" name="productId" value="42">
  <input type="number" name="qty" value="1">
  <button>Buy</button>
</form>

// OUTPUT:
// POST /checkout  body: productId=42&qty=1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of the technique:

  • GET form: hidden values appear in the URL and in logs.
  • POST form: values go in the body, better for larger or private data.
  • Many values: use several hidden inputs, or one input with an encoded string.
  • Arrays: repeat the same name and read with getParameterValues.

intermediate.content:
How Hidden Form Fields Work

• The server embeds data into hidden input fields inside a form. When the form is submitted, the hidden data is sent along with other form parameters.


Important Points

  • • Data is visible in page source
  • • Data can be modified using browser developer tools
  • • Works only with form submission

Advantages

  • • No dependency on cookies
  • • Easy to implement

Disadvantages

  • • Security risks (data tampering)
  • • Works only when form is submitted
  • • Not suitable for large data

expert.content:
Security Considerations

• Hidden fields are not secure because users can modify them using browser developer tools.


Common Risks

  • • Parameter Tampering
  • • Privilege Escalation
  • • Data Manipulation

Best Practices

  • • Never store sensitive data in hidden fields
  • • Validate all data on the server side
  • • Use server-side session (HttpSession) for secure data
  • • Use CSRF tokens for form security

When to Use Hidden Fields?

• Hidden fields are suitable for small, non-sensitive data that needs to be passed between form submissions.
• They should not replace secure session management mechanisms.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Multi-step wizard: every page re-posts the earlier answers as hidden fields, and the last page submits everything together.
  • Limits: works only with form submits (POST or GET), not with plain links, and every page must be generated dynamically.
  • Versus other techniques: cookies and HttpSession keep data on the server or browser across all pages, hidden fields only across a chain of forms.

Senior Notes

  • Tampering: a user can change price or userId in a hidden field, so re-read the real value from the database on the server.
  • Signing: when you must round-trip data, add an HMAC over the value or store it in the session and send only a random token.
  • CSRF token: a hidden field holding a per-session random token is the standard defence against cross-site request forgery.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Trusting price or role: reload from the database.
  • Unescaped output: a value containing a quote breaks the HTML or enables XSS; escape it.
  • Secrets in hidden fields: they are visible in the page source.
  • Lost state: a page reached by a link, not a form, drops the values.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Hidden fields cost nothing on the server, but large ones slow every page.

  • Page weight: each field is sent again on every submit.
  • Alternative: past a few hundred bytes keep the data in the session and send an id.
  • Signing cost: an HMAC is cheap compared with a database call.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a three-page registration wizard.

  • Design: store partial answers in the session, and use hidden fields only for the step number and a CSRF token.
  • Back button: the step field lets the server detect out-of-order posts.

beginner.content:
What is Session Tracking?

• Session Tracking is a mechanism used to maintain user-specific data across multiple HTTP requests.

• Since HTTP is stateless, session tracking helps identify a user between requests.


Main Session Tracking Techniques

  • • Cookies
  • • URL Rewriting
  • • Hidden Form Fields
  • • HttpSession (Server-side session)

Fresher Notes

  • Four techniques: cookies, URL rewriting, hidden form fields and HttpSession. Each one tries to link many requests to one user.
  • Where data lives: cookies and hidden fields keep data on the client, HttpSession keeps data on the server and sends only an id.
  • Default choice: use HttpSession, which normally uses a cookie named JSESSIONID and falls back to URL rewriting.

Worked Example 1

Login with session fixation protection.

Worked Example 2

Choosing by need.

Practice Exercise 1

Using encodeURL for cookie-less browsers.

Practice Exercise 2

Setting a safe cookie.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

All techniques give the server a key that identifies the client.

  • Cookie: the browser stores JSESSIONID and sends it in the Cookie header.
  • URL rewriting: the id is added to the path as ;jsessionid=....
  • Hidden field: the id or state sits in the form body.
  • HttpSession: the container maps the id to a server-side map of attributes.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Comparison at a glance:

  • Cookies: client store, any page, can be blocked.
  • URL rewriting: any client, ids leak in URLs.
  • Hidden fields: form chains only, no cookies needed.
  • HttpSession: server store, full objects, uses one of the other three to carry the id.
codeExamples:
<!-- Technique      Stores on   Survives restart  Needs cookies
     Cookie         client      yes (max age)     yes
     URL rewriting  URL         no                no
     Hidden field   page        no                no
     HttpSession    server      no                usually -->

<!-- OUTPUT: a summary table only, nothing is executed. -->

intermediate.content:
Comparison Table

Technique Storage Location Security Works Without Cookies?
Cookies Client-side (Browser) Medium No
URL Rewriting URL Low Yes
Hidden Fields HTML Form Low Yes
HttpSession Server-side High Yes (with URL rewriting fallback)

Quick Explanation

  • • Cookies: Stored in browser, sent automatically with each request.
  • • URL Rewriting: Session ID appended to URL.
  • • Hidden Fields: Data passed through form submission.
  • • HttpSession: Secure server-side session storage.

expert.content:
Detailed Technical Comparison

1. Cookies

  • • Stored in browser memory or disk
  • • Limited size (~4KB)
  • • Can be disabled by user
  • • Can use HttpOnly & Secure flags

2. URL Rewriting

  • • Session ID visible in URL
  • • Risk of session hijacking
  • • Not suitable for sensitive applications

3. Hidden Form Fields

  • • Works only with form submission
  • • Data can be modified using browser tools

4. HttpSession

  • • Stores data on server
  • • More secure
  • • Supports session timeout
  • • Scalable using distributed session management

Best Practice Recommendation

• For modern applications, use HttpSession or token-based authentication (like JWT).
• Use URL rewriting only as a fallback when cookies are disabled.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Cookies work on every page and survive browser restarts if given a max age, but users can disable them and they are limited to about 4 KB each.
  • URL rewriting works when cookies are off, but ids show up in logs, bookmarks and the Referer header.
  • Hidden fields need a form on every page and carry data only along a form chain.

Senior Notes

  • Security: prefer HttpOnly and Secure cookies, and avoid session ids in URLs to prevent session fixation and leaks.
  • Scaling: server sessions need sticky routing, replication or an external store such as Redis. Signed tokens (JWT) move state to the client.
  • Hybrid: keep identity in the session, keep small preferences in a long-lived cookie, and use hidden tokens for CSRF.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Cookie without HttpOnly: scripts can steal it.
  • Large objects in the session: memory grows per user.
  • No logout invalidate: call session.invalidate().
  • Non-serializable attributes: replication and restarts fail.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Timeout: set session-timeout to the real need, not hours.
  • Lazy creation: use getSession(false) on public pages so crawlers do not create sessions.
  • Size: keep only ids and small objects.
  • Clustering: prefer an external store for many nodes.
codeExamples:
<session-config>
  <session-timeout>15</session-timeout>
  <cookie-config><http-only>true</http-only><secure>true</secure></cookie-config>
  <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode>
</session-config>

<!-- OUTPUT:
15 minute idle timeout, safe cookie, no URL rewriting. -->

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an online shop.

  • Cart: in the session.
  • Guest preferences: a 90 day cookie for language.
  • Checkout CSRF: hidden token.
  • Mobile apps: signed tokens in a header instead of cookies.

beginner.content:
What is web.xml?

• web.xml is called the Deployment Descriptor of a Java Web Application.
• It is an XML configuration file that defines how the web application should behave inside the servlet container.

• It is located inside the WEB-INF folder and cannot be accessed directly from the browser.


Why is it Important?

  • • Central configuration file for web applications
  • • Controls request routing
  • • Defines lifecycle behavior
  • • Manages session settings

Main Responsibilities

  • • Configure Servlets
  • • Map URLs to Servlets
  • • Configure Filters & Listeners
  • • Define Welcome Files
  • • Session Configuration
  • • Error Handling

When is web.xml Loaded?

• It is loaded when the server starts or when the application is deployed.
codeExamples:
<!-- Basic web.xml structure -->
<web-app xmlns="http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/javaee"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/javaee
         http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/javaee/web-app_3_1.xsd"
         version="3.1">

</web-app>

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • web.xml is the deployment descriptor in WEB-INF/. It tells the container which servlets, filters, listeners and settings the application uses.
  • Root element is <web-app>. Inside go <servlet>, <servlet-mapping>, <welcome-file-list> and more.
  • Optional since Servlet 3.0: annotations such as @WebServlet can replace most entries.

Worked Example 1

Same servlet with an annotation.

Worked Example 2

Security constraint.
codeExamples:
<security-constraint>
  <web-resource-collection>
    <web-resource-name>Admin</web-resource-name>
    <url-pattern>/admin/*</url-pattern>
  </web-resource-collection>
  <auth-constraint><role-name>admin</role-name></auth-constraint>
</security-constraint>

<!-- OUTPUT:
Anyone opening /admin/* must log in with the admin role. -->

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Minimal web.xml with welcome file and error page.
codeExamples:
<web-app xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee" version="6.0">
  <servlet>
    <servlet-name>Hello</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>com.example.HelloServlet</servlet-class>
  </servlet>
  <servlet-mapping>
    <servlet-name>Hello</servlet-name>
    <url-pattern>/hello</url-pattern>
  </servlet-mapping>
  <welcome-file-list><welcome-file>index.html</welcome-file></welcome-file-list>
  <error-page><error-code>404</error-code><location>/404.html</location></error-page>
</web-app>

<!-- OUTPUT:
GET /app/        -> index.html
GET /app/hello   -> HelloServlet
GET /app/nothing -> 404.html -->

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Session timeout and listener.
codeExamples:
<session-config><session-timeout>20</session-timeout></session-config>
<listener><listener-class>com.example.AppStartListener</listener-class></listener>

<!-- OUTPUT:
Sessions expire after 20 idle minutes;
AppStartListener runs at startup. -->

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container reads the descriptor at deployment.

  • Parse: web.xml is validated against the schema and merged with annotations and web-fragment.xml files.
  • Build: it creates servlet definitions, mappings, filters in order and listeners.
  • Startup: listeners fire, then servlets with load-on-startup are initialized in ascending order.
  • Lazy: others are created at the first request.
codeExamples:
<servlet>
  <servlet-name>Warm</servlet-name>
  <servlet-class>com.example.WarmServlet</servlet-class>
  <load-on-startup>2</load-on-startup>
</servlet>

<!-- OUTPUT: (varies)
INFO: WarmServlet init called during deployment, before any request. -->

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Main elements and options:

  • welcome-file-list: tried in order for directory URLs.
  • filter and filter-mapping: by url-pattern or servlet-name, with dispatcher types.
  • error-page: by status code or exception type.
  • mime-mapping: extension to content type.
  • session-config: timeout, cookie settings, tracking modes.
  • display-name: label for tools.
codeExamples:
<error-page>
  <exception-type>java.lang.IllegalStateException</exception-type>
  <location>/error.jsp</location>
</error-page>
<mime-mapping><extension>json</extension><mime-type>application/json</mime-type></mime-mapping>
<welcome-file-list>
  <welcome-file>index.jsp</welcome-file>
  <welcome-file>index.html</welcome-file>
</welcome-file-list>

<!-- OUTPUT:
GET / serves index.jsp if it exists, else index.html. -->

intermediate.content:
Servlet Configuration in web.xml


1. Define Servlet

• Register the servlet class inside web.xml.


2. Map URL Pattern

• Map a URL to the servlet.


3. Initialization Parameters

• You can define servlet-specific parameters using <init-param>.


4. Welcome File List

• Defines the default page when user accesses application root.


5. Session Timeout

• Defines session expiration time (in minutes).


6. MIME Mapping

• Used to define custom file extension types.
codeExamples:
<!-- Servlet Declaration with Init Params -->
<servlet>
    <servlet-name>MyServlet</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>com.example.MyServlet</servlet-class>
    <init-param>
        <param-name>message</param-name>
        <param-value>Hello World</param-value>
    </init-param>
</servlet>

<!-- Servlet Mapping -->
<servlet-mapping>
    <servlet-name>MyServlet</servlet-name>
    <url-pattern>/home</url-pattern>
</servlet-mapping>

<!-- Welcome File Configuration -->
<welcome-file-list>
    <welcome-file>index.jsp</welcome-file>
    <welcome-file>home.jsp</welcome-file>
</welcome-file-list>

<!-- Session Timeout -->
<session-config>
    <session-timeout>30</session-timeout>
</session-config>

<!-- MIME Mapping -->
<mime-mapping>
    <extension>pdf</extension>
    <mime-type>application/pdf</mime-type>
</mime-mapping>

expert.content:
Advanced web.xml Configuration


1. Filter Configuration

• Filters intercept requests and responses before reaching servlet.
• Used for authentication, logging, compression, etc.


2. Listener Configuration

• Listeners monitor application, session, and request lifecycle events.


3. Error Page Configuration

• Custom error pages can be configured for specific HTTP errors or Java exceptions.


4. Context Parameters

• Global configuration parameters accessible via ServletContext.


5. Security Configuration

• Declarative security can be defined using security constraints.


6. Ordering & Metadata

• Using metadata-complete="true" disables annotation scanning.


Annotation vs web.xml

  • • Servlet 3.0+ supports annotations (@WebServlet, @WebFilter)
  • • web.xml provides centralized configuration
  • • Preferred in large enterprise applications
  • • Annotations reduce XML boilerplate

Best Practices

  • • Keep configuration clean and organized
  • • Use web.xml for production-grade centralized config
  • • Combine annotations and XML wisely
  • • Document complex configurations
codeExamples:
<!-- Filter Configuration -->
<filter>
    <filter-name>AuthFilter</filter-name>
    <filter-class>com.example.AuthFilter</filter-class>
</filter>

<filter-mapping>
    <filter-name>AuthFilter</filter-name>
    <url-pattern>/*</url-pattern>
</filter-mapping>

<!-- Listener Configuration -->
<listener>
    <listener-class>com.example.AppListener</listener-class>
</listener>

<!-- Error Page Configuration (Exception Based) -->
<error-page>
    <exception-type>java.lang.Exception</exception-type>
    <location>/error.jsp</location>
</error-page>

<!-- Security Constraint -->
<security-constraint>
    <web-resource-collection>
        <web-resource-name>Admin Area</web-resource-name>
        <url-pattern>/admin/*</url-pattern>
    </web-resource-collection>
    <auth-constraint>
        <role-name>ADMIN</role-name>
    </auth-constraint>
</security-constraint>

<!-- Disable Annotation Scanning -->
<web-app metadata-complete="true" version="3.1"
         xmlns="http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/javaee">
</web-app>

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Welcome files: <welcome-file-list> picks the page served for a directory URL such as /. The first existing file wins.
  • Other entries: <context-param>, <filter>, <listener>, <session-config>, <error-page>, <security-constraint>.
  • Namespaces: Tomcat 9 uses javax.servlet and the Java EE schema; Tomcat 10 and Jakarta EE 9+ use jakarta.servlet and the Jakarta schema.

Senior Notes

  • web.xml versus annotations: web.xml wins when both set the same thing, and only web.xml can change settings without recompiling.
  • metadata-complete: metadata-complete="true" stops annotation scanning, which speeds startup. web-fragment.xml in libraries adds parts.
  • Ordering: filters run in the order their mappings appear in web.xml; with annotations the order is not defined.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong schema or version: an old 2.3 DTD turns off newer features such as EL.
  • Servlet-name mismatch: mapping name differs from the servlet name, so deployment fails.
  • Missing leading slash: url-pattern hello is invalid; use /hello.
  • Duplicate mapping: same pattern for two servlets.
  • javax versus jakarta: a class built for the wrong package fails with ClassNotFoundException.
codeExamples:
<!-- WRONG -->
<servlet-mapping><servlet-name>Hello</servlet-name><url-pattern>hello</url-pattern></servlet-mapping>
<!-- RIGHT -->
<servlet-mapping><servlet-name>Hello</servlet-name><url-pattern>/hello</url-pattern></servlet-mapping>

<!-- OUTPUT:
WRONG: Invalid <url-pattern> hello in servlet mapping (container message varies). -->

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning with the descriptor:

  • metadata-complete: skips class scanning for faster start.
  • load-on-startup: moves slow initialization out of the first request.
  • absolute-ordering: controls fragment order and scanning.
  • Compression and caching: usually set in the container, not in web.xml.
codeExamples:
<web-app xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee" version="6.0"
         metadata-complete="true">
  <absolute-ordering/>
</web-app>

<!-- OUTPUT: (varies)
Startup is faster;
annotations like @WebServlet are no longer scanned. -->

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: moving from XML to annotations.

  • Keep in XML: security, error pages, session config, filter order.
  • Move to annotations: simple servlets and listeners.
  • Rule: one place per setting, to avoid surprises when XML overrides annotation.

beginner.content:
What is Servlet Mapping?

• Servlet Mapping is the process of associating a URL pattern with a specific servlet class.

• When a client sends a request to a particular URL, the servlet container routes the request to the mapped servlet.


Why is Mapping Required?

  • • To connect browser URL with servlet class
  • • To handle client requests properly
  • • To avoid direct access to class files
  • • To define clear request handling logic

Where is Mapping Defined?

  • • Inside web.xml file (Deployment Descriptor)
  • • Using @WebServlet annotation (Servlet 3.0+)

Basic Flow

  1. • User enters URL
  2. • Servlet container checks mapping
  3. • Matching servlet is executed
codeExamples:
<!-- web.xml Example -->
<servlet>
    <servlet-name>MyServlet</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>com.example.MyServlet</servlet-class>
</servlet>

<servlet-mapping>
    <servlet-name>MyServlet</servlet-name>
    <url-pattern>/home</url-pattern>
</servlet-mapping>

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Servlet mapping links a URL pattern to a servlet, so a request for /hello reaches the right class.
  • Pattern types: exact (/hello), path prefix (/api/*), extension (*.do) and default (/).
  • Annotation form: @WebServlet("/hello") does the same as the web.xml pair.

Worked Example 1

Multiple mappings.

Worked Example 2

Longest prefix wins.
codeExamples:
<!-- /api/* -> Generic,  /api/admin/* -> Admin -->
<!-- OUTPUT:
GET /api/admin/users -> Admin   (longer prefix)
GET /api/orders      -> Generic -->

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Matching examples.
codeExamples:
<!-- patterns:  /shop  /shop/*  *.do  /  -->
<!-- OUTPUT:
/shop        -> exact /shop
/shop/cart   -> /shop/*  (path prefix)
/login.do    -> *.do     (extension)
/logo.png    -> /        (default servlet, static file) -->

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Reading path parts.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container matches the request path, after removing the context path, in a fixed order.

  • 1. Exact: the whole path equals a pattern.
  • 2. Path prefix: the longest pattern ending in /* that matches.
  • 3. Extension: the last segment ends with the *.ext suffix.
  • 4. Default: the servlet mapped to /. If none, the container built-in one serves files.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Pattern rules:

  • Exact: starts with /, no wildcard.
  • Prefix: starts with / and ends with /*.
  • Extension: starts with *. with no slash.
  • Empty string: maps the context root only.
  • Welcome files: a directory request is first mapped, then the welcome list is tried.
codeExamples:
<servlet-mapping>
  <servlet-name>Root</servlet-name>
  <url-pattern></url-pattern>
</servlet-mapping>

<!-- OUTPUT:
Only GET /app (the context root) goes to Root, not /app/anything. -->

intermediate.content:
Types of URL Patterns in Servlet Mapping

1. Exact Match

• /home → Matches exactly /home


2. Path Mapping

• /admin/* → Matches all URLs under /admin


3. Extension Mapping

• *.do → Matches all URLs ending with .do


4. Default Mapping

• / → Handles all unmatched requests


Multiple URL Patterns

• A single servlet can handle multiple URL patterns.


Load on Startup

• Using <load-on-startup> element in web.xml, servlet can be loaded when server starts.


Servlet 3.0 Annotation-Based Mapping

• Instead of web.xml, we can use @WebServlet annotation.
codeExamples:
<!-- Load on Startup -->
<servlet>
    <servlet-name>InitServlet</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>com.example.InitServlet</servlet-class>
    <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
</servlet>

expert.content:
How Servlet Container Resolves Mapping

• When multiple mappings match a request, the servlet container follows this priority order:

  1. • Exact Match
  2. • Longest Path Match
  3. • Extension Match
  4. • Default Servlet

Mapping Conflict Handling

  • • Duplicate URL patterns cause deployment errors
  • • web.xml configuration overrides annotations if metadata-complete="true"

Performance Considerations

  • • Exact match is fastest
  • • Avoid excessive wildcard mappings
  • • Organize URL hierarchy logically

Security Considerations

  • • Use secure URL naming conventions
  • • Restrict sensitive paths via filter or security constraints

Best Practices

  • • Use REST-style URL patterns
  • • Keep mappings readable and meaningful
  • • Prefer annotations for modern applications
  • • Use web.xml for centralized enterprise configuration

Common Mistakes

  • • Duplicate URL patterns
  • • Incorrect path syntax
  • • Mapping conflicts between web.xml and annotations
  • • Using /* unintentionally (overrides other mappings)
codeExamples:
<!-- Security Constraint Example -->
<security-constraint>
    <web-resource-collection>
        <web-resource-name>Admin Area</web-resource-name>
        <url-pattern>/admin/*</url-pattern>
    </web-resource-collection>
</security-constraint>

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Precedence: exact match first, then the longest path prefix, then extension, then the default servlet.
  • Several patterns: one servlet can have many mappings, for example /a and /b.
  • Path info: for /api/users/5 matched by /api/*, getServletPath() is /api and getPathInfo() is /users/5.

Senior Notes

  • Default servlet: the pattern / catches everything not matched, and the container serves static files with it. /* is different and overrides everything, even JSPs.
  • Conflicts: two servlets with the same pattern make the deployment fail or behave unpredictably.
  • Modern routing: frameworks use one front controller on /* or / and route inside, as Spring DispatcherServlet does.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Using /* for a servlet: JSPs and static files stop working.
  • Extension with a slash: /*.do is invalid; use *.do.
  • Forgetting the context path in links: use req.getContextPath().
  • Relative links after path-info: /api/x/y changes how relative links resolve.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Matching is cheap. The container builds a lookup structure at startup, so request cost does not grow noticeably with mappings.

  • Keep patterns specific: clearer and avoids shadowing.
  • Static assets: serve through the default servlet or a CDN, not through your front controller.
  • Filters: map them narrowly so they do not run on images.
codeExamples:
<filter-mapping>
  <filter-name>AuthFilter</filter-name>
  <url-pattern>/secure/*</url-pattern>
  <dispatcher>REQUEST</dispatcher>
</filter-mapping>

<!-- OUTPUT:
AuthFilter runs only for /secure/* requests. -->

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a REST style API on a plain servlet.

  • Map: /api/*.
  • Route: split getPathInfo() inside the servlet.
  • Static site: left to the default servlet.

beginner.content:
What are Init Parameters?
