• Init Parameters (Initialization Parameters) are configuration values provided to a servlet during initialization.

• They are defined in web.xml and accessed inside the servlet using the ServletConfig object.


Why Use Init Parameters?

  • • To provide configuration without hardcoding values
  • • To make application flexible
  • • To separate configuration from business logic
  • • To change values without modifying source code

Types of Init Parameters

  • • Servlet-specific Init Parameters
  • • Context-wide (Global) Parameters

Key Point

• Init parameters are read-only and available after servlet initialization.
codeExamples:
<!-- Servlet-specific Init Parameter -->
<servlet>
    <servlet-name>MyServlet</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>com.example.MyServlet</servlet-class>

    <init-param>
        <param-name>message</param-name>
        <param-value>Hello User</param-value>
    </init-param>
</servlet>

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Init parameter is a name/value setting given to one servlet, read with getInitParameter("name") from ServletConfig.
  • Set in web.xml with <init-param> inside <servlet>, or with @WebInitParam in an annotation.
  • Private to that servlet: another servlet cannot see it. For app-wide values use context parameters.

Worked Example 1

Listing all init parameters.

Worked Example 2

Safe default.

Practice Exercise 1

web.xml init-param and servlet.
codeExamples:
<servlet>
  <servlet-name>Mail</servlet-name>
  <servlet-class>com.example.MailServlet</servlet-class>
  <init-param>
    <param-name>sender</param-name>
    <param-value>noreply@example.com</param-value>
  </init-param>
</servlet>

public class MailServlet extends HttpServlet {
    private String sender;
    @Override public void init() {
        sender = getInitParameter("sender");
    }
}

<!-- OUTPUT:
sender field holds noreply@example.com after init. -->

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Annotation form.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How init parameters reach the servlet:

  • Parse: the container reads init-param entries into a map for that servlet.
  • Create: it builds a ServletConfig holding the map and the context.
  • Init: it calls init(config); GenericServlet stores the config so getInitParameter works.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options:

  • web.xml: several init-param blocks, each with an optional description.
  • Annotation: @WebInitParam inside initParams.
  • Programmatic: ServletContext.addServlet then setInitParameter in a listener.
  • Override: web.xml beats the annotation.

intermediate.content:
ServletConfig vs ServletContext Parameters

1. Servlet-Specific Init Parameters

  • • Defined inside <servlet> tag
  • • Accessible using ServletConfig
  • • Available only to that servlet

2. Context Parameters (Global)

  • • Defined using <context-param>
  • • Accessible using ServletContext
  • • Shared across entire application

3. Lifecycle Understanding

  • • init() method is called only once
  • • Parameters are loaded at servlet startup
  • • Useful for loading configuration resources

4. Access Methods

  • • getServletConfig().getInitParameter()
  • • getServletContext().getInitParameter()
codeExamples:
<!-- Context Parameter (Global) -->
<context-param>
    <param-name>dbUrl</param-name>
    <param-value>jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/testdb</param-value>
</context-param>

expert.content:
Advanced Usage of Init Parameters

1. Real-World Use Cases

  • • Database configuration (URL, driver name)
  • • Email server configuration
  • • File upload directory path
  • • Application constants

2. Load-on-Startup with Init Parameters

• When combined with <load-on-startup>, configuration can be loaded immediately during server startup.


3. Lifecycle & Performance

  • • Init parameters are immutable
  • • Loaded once per servlet lifecycle
  • • Improves performance by avoiding repeated configuration loading

4. Security Considerations

  • • Avoid storing passwords in web.xml
  • • Use environment variables for sensitive data
  • • Consider external configuration files (.properties)

5. Annotation-Based Init Parameters

• Init parameters can also be defined using @WebInitParam annotation.


6. Best Practices

  • • Use context parameters for shared settings
  • • Use servlet init parameters for servlet-specific configs
  • • Document parameter usage clearly
codeExamples:
<!-- Load on Startup Example -->
<servlet>
    <servlet-name>StartupServlet</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>com.example.StartupServlet</servlet-class>
    <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
</servlet>

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • When read: the container calls init(ServletConfig) once, so read the values there and store them in fields.
  • Type: values are always Strings. Convert with Integer.parseInt and handle a missing value (null).
  • Use cases: a database name, page size, email sender address, feature flag per servlet.

Senior Notes

  • Config without recompiling: change web.xml and redeploy; keep secrets out and use environment variables or a vault instead.
  • Defaults: always provide a fallback when getInitParameter returns null, and fail fast in init if a value is mandatory.
  • Thread safety: values read in init and not changed are safe to share between request threads.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Overriding init(ServletConfig) without super: config is lost; override init() instead.
  • Reading in doGet each time: wasteful; read once.
  • NumberFormatException: a bad value crashes init; the servlet is then unavailable.
  • Wrong place: param under context-param is not visible through ServletConfig.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Cache: copy values to final fields in init.
  • Fail fast: check mandatory values during startup.
  • Startup order: use load-on-startup to see errors at deploy time.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: one servlet class reused with different settings.

  • Two registrations: the same class under two names, each with its own init-params and mappings.
codeExamples:
<servlet><servlet-name>Small</servlet-name><servlet-class>com.example.Grid</servlet-class>
  <init-param><param-name>rows</param-name><param-value>5</param-value></init-param></servlet>
<servlet><servlet-name>Big</servlet-name><servlet-class>com.example.Grid</servlet-class>
  <init-param><param-name>rows</param-name><param-value>50</param-value></init-param></servlet>

<!-- OUTPUT:
Two instances of Grid exist, one with rows=5 and one with rows=50. -->

beginner.content:
What are Context Parameters?

• Context Parameters are global initialization parameters defined in web.xml that are accessible to the entire web application.

• They are configured using the <context-param> tag and accessed using the ServletContext object.


Why Use Context Parameters?

  • • To store application-wide configuration
  • • To avoid hardcoding values
  • • To share configuration across multiple servlets

Important Point

• Context parameters are available to all servlets, JSPs, and filters.
codeExamples:
<!-- Defining Context Parameter -->
<context-param>
    <param-name>appName</param-name>
    <param-value>MyWebApplication</param-value>
</context-param>

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Context parameter is an application-wide setting, defined with <context-param> directly under <web-app>.
  • Read with getServletContext().getInitParameter("name"). Every servlet, filter and JSP in the app can read it.
  • Versus init-param: init-param belongs to one servlet through ServletConfig; context-param belongs to the whole app through ServletContext.

Worked Example 1

Config versus context side by side.

Worked Example 2

Listing context parameters.

Practice Exercise 1

Define and read a context parameter.
codeExamples:
<context-param>
  <param-name>appName</param-name>
  <param-value>JavaSchoolLab</param-value>
</context-param>

ServletContext ctx = getServletContext();
String app = ctx.getInitParameter("appName");
System.out.println(app);

// OUTPUT:
// JavaSchoolLab

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Listener using it at startup.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

How they work:

  • Load: the container reads every context-param into the single ServletContext of the app.
  • Access: any component calls getServletContext().getInitParameter.
  • Immutable: the API has no setter for parameters after startup (a listener may call setInitParameter before the context starts).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and related tools:

  • context-param: String configuration.
  • Context attribute: setAttribute, any object, changes at run time.
  • env-entry and JNDI: typed values from the server.
  • Properties file: load with getResourceAsStream.

intermediate.content:
Context Parameters vs Init Parameters

1. Context Parameters

  • • Defined using <context-param>
  • • Accessible using ServletContext
  • • Shared across entire application

2. Servlet Init Parameters

  • • Defined inside <servlet>
  • • Accessible using ServletConfig
  • • Specific to a single servlet

Lifecycle Behavior

  • • Loaded when application starts
  • • Available until application stops
  • • Immutable during runtime

Common Use Cases

  • • Database URL
  • • Application name
  • • Email server configuration
  • • File storage path
codeExamples:
<!-- Multiple Context Parameters -->
<context-param>
    <param-name>dbUrl</param-name>
    <param-value>jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/testdb</param-value>
</context-param>

<context-param>
    <param-name>supportEmail</param-name>
    <param-value>support@example.com</param-value>
</context-param>

expert.content:
Advanced Concepts of Context Parameters

1. Application Scope

• Context parameters exist at application scope and are shared across all servlets, filters, and listeners.


2. Performance Consideration

  • • Loaded once at application startup
  • • Efficient for static configuration values

3. Security Considerations

  • • Do not store sensitive data like passwords
  • • Prefer external configuration files or environment variables

4. Using with Listeners

• Context parameters are often used inside ServletContextListener to initialize resources (like DB connections) during application startup.


5. Annotation-Based Alternative

• Using @WebListener with ServletContextListener allows reading context parameters without relying only on web.xml.


Best Practices

  • • Use for shared configuration only
  • • Keep values environment-specific
  • • Document parameter usage clearly

Mid-Level Notes

  • Read only: context parameters cannot be changed at run time. For shared changing data use setAttribute on the context.
  • Typical values: database URL, application name, default locale, admin e-mail.
  • Listener: read them in a ServletContextListener at startup to build shared resources such as a connection pool.

Senior Notes

  • Parameter versus attribute: parameters are String configuration from the descriptor; attributes are live objects set by code and need thread-safe handling.
  • Environment: use different values per environment with overrides (system properties, JNDI env-entry) instead of editing the war.
  • Secrets: never keep passwords in plain context-param; use JNDI datasources or a secret store.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes:

  • Placing the tag inside a servlet element: then it is an init-param; context-param belongs under web-app.
  • Mixing up the two getInitParameter calls: ServletConfig versus ServletContext.
  • Mutable shared state: attributes need synchronization or concurrent classes.
  • Secrets: plain text in web.xml.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Read once: at startup in a listener, and keep a parsed config object.
  • Concurrent attributes: store immutable or concurrent objects.
  • Restart cost: changing a context-param needs a redeploy or reload.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: one war for three environments.

  • Defaults: put safe values in web.xml.
  • Overrides: read system properties or environment variables first.
  • Result: the same artifact is promoted from test to production.

beginner.content:
What is @WebServlet?

• @WebServlet is an annotation introduced in Servlet 3.0 that allows servlet configuration directly inside the servlet class instead of configuring it inside web.xml.

• It is part of annotation-based configuration which simplifies web application development.


Why Was @WebServlet Introduced?

  • • To reduce heavy XML configuration
  • • To make configuration closer to code
  • • To simplify small and medium-sized applications

Basic Syntax

• @WebServlet("/urlPattern")


How It Works

  1. • Server starts
  2. • Container scans classes for annotations
  3. • Servlet is automatically registered

Fresher Notes

  • @WebServlet registers a servlet without web.xml: @WebServlet("/hello") on a class that extends HttpServlet.
  • URL patterns can be exact (/hello), a path (/api/*) or an extension (*.do).
  • Packages: Jakarta EE 9+ (Tomcat 10+) uses jakarta.servlet.*; Java EE and Tomcat 9 use javax.servlet.*.

Worked Example 1

Three pattern types.

Worked Example 2

Duplicate mapping failure.

Practice Exercise 1

A first annotated servlet.

Practice Exercise 2

Init parameters and startup order.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container finds annotated classes at deployment time.

  • Scanning: Tomcat scans WEB-INF/classes and jars in WEB-INF/lib for @WebServlet, @WebFilter and @WebListener.
  • Merge: annotation metadata is merged with web.xml; the descriptor wins on conflicts for the same name.
  • Mapping: patterns go into a mapper: exact first, then longest path prefix, then extension, then the default servlet.
  • Lifecycle: one instance per declaration, created lazily unless loadOnStartup is set.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options of the annotation:

  • value / urlPatterns: alias of each other; use one only.
  • name: servlet name used in logs and by servletNames filter mappings.
  • initParams: array of @WebInitParam.
  • loadOnStartup: negative means lazy.
  • asyncSupported: required for startAsync().
  • @MultipartConfig: a separate annotation for file upload.

intermediate.content:
@WebServlet Attributes Explained

• @WebServlet supports multiple configuration attributes:

  • • name – Logical name of the servlet
  • • urlPatterns / value – URL mapping
  • • initParams – Initialization parameters
  • • loadOnStartup – Load priority at startup
  • • asyncSupported – Enables asynchronous processing

Multiple URL Patterns

• A single servlet can respond to multiple URL endpoints.


Asynchronous Support

• asyncSupported = true allows non-blocking request processing.


Load On Startup Behavior

  • • 0 or positive → Loaded at startup
  • • Negative or default → Loaded on first request

expert.content:
Deep Dive into @WebServlet

1. Annotation Processing Mechanism

• During application startup, the servlet container scans all classes inside WEB-INF/classes and JAR files inside WEB-INF/lib.
• If it finds @WebServlet, it registers the servlet automatically.

2. Annotation vs web.xml Priority

  • • If both exist, web.xml configuration overrides annotation.
  • • If metadata-complete="true" is set in web.xml, annotation scanning is disabled.

3. Mapping Resolution Rules

  • • Exact match has highest priority
  • • Longest path match next
  • • Extension mapping next
  • • Default mapping last

4. Async Processing Example

• Useful for long-running tasks like file uploads, external API calls, etc.


5. Limitations

  • • No centralized configuration file
  • • Harder to manage in large enterprise apps
  • • May increase startup time due to class scanning

6. Best Practices

  • • Use clear and REST-style URL patterns
  • • Avoid duplicate mappings
  • • Use packages to organize servlets logically
  • • Combine annotations with filters and listeners wisely

Enterprise Recommendation

• Small Projects → Prefer annotations • Large Enterprise Systems → Combine web.xml + annotations strategically
codeExamples:
<!-- metadata-complete Example -->
<web-app metadata-complete="true"
         xmlns="http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/javaee"
         version="3.1">
</web-app>

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Attributes: name, urlPatterns, initParams, loadOnStartup and asyncSupported are the common ones.
  • Init parameters go in @WebInitParam(name, value) and are read with getInitParameter.
  • Conflicts: two servlets mapped to the same pattern make the application fail to start, so keep patterns unique.

Senior Notes

  • Precedence: a web.xml entry for the same servlet name overrides the annotation, which helps per-environment tuning.
  • metadata-complete: metadata-complete="true" in web.xml turns annotation scanning off, and it also speeds up startup.
  • Startup cost: the container scans classes for annotations, so keep jars out of WEB-INF/lib that you do not need, or use web-fragment excludes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Wrong package: javax.servlet annotations on Tomcat 10 are ignored; use jakarta.servlet there.
  • Missing leading slash: "hello" is invalid and fails deployment.
  • Both value and urlPatterns: not allowed.
  • Duplicate mappings across classes or with web.xml.
  • metadata-complete=true left in an old descriptor, so annotations silently do nothing.
  • Instance state: servlet fields are shared by all threads.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning startup and runtime:

  • Scan less: metadata-complete or Tomcat jarsToSkip shortens startup.
  • Warm up: use loadOnStartup for servlets with costly init so the first user does not wait.
  • Stateless: a stateless servlet scales well on the thread pool.
  • Async: use asyncSupported for long-polling, not for short work.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world layout of a small app: one servlet per feature area, a path mapping for an API, and web.xml only for environment settings.

  • /api/*: one front servlet, dispatches on getPathInfo().
  • Pages: exact mappings that forward to JSP under WEB-INF.
  • Config: context-params and welcome files in web.xml.

beginner.content:
What is a Filter?

• A Filter is a server-side component in the Java Servlet API that intercepts client requests and responses before they reach a servlet or after leaving a servlet.


Purpose of Filters

  • • Pre-processing requests (e.g., authentication, logging)
  • • Post-processing responses (e.g., compression, encoding)
  • • Separation of cross-cutting concerns

Filter Lifecycle

  • • init() – Called once when filter is first loaded
  • • doFilter() – Called for every request/response
  • • destroy() – Called before filter removal

Execution Flow

• Client → Filter → Servlet → Filter → Client

Fresher Notes

  • Filter is a component that runs before and after a servlet, so it can inspect or change the request and the response.
  • Typical uses: logging, authentication, compression, character encoding and CORS headers.
  • Declaration: put @WebFilter("/*") on a class that implements jakarta.servlet.Filter.

Worked Example 1

Blocking with a filter.

Worked Example 2

Order in web.xml.
codeExamples:
<filter-mapping><filter-name>Encoding</filter-name>
  <url-pattern>/*</url-pattern></filter-mapping>
<filter-mapping><filter-name>Auth</filter-name>
  <url-pattern>/*</url-pattern></filter-mapping>
<filter-mapping><filter-name>Timing</filter-name>
  <url-pattern>/*</url-pattern></filter-mapping>

// OUTPUT:
// request path : Encoding -> Auth -> Timing -> servlet
// response path: servlet -> Timing -> Auth -> Encoding

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

A request timing filter.

Practice Exercise 2

Setting character encoding.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Filters are a chain of responsibility built by the container for each request.

  • Matching: the container picks filters whose URL or servlet mapping matches and whose dispatcher type fits.
  • Chain: a FilterChain holds them in order; each chain.doFilter moves to the next, and the last one calls servlet.service.
  • Order: web.xml URL mappings in declaration order, then servlet-name mappings. Annotation order is unspecified, often by class name.
  • Unwinding: code after chain.doFilter runs in reverse.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of declaration:

  • @WebFilter: urlPatterns, servletNames, dispatcherTypes, initParams.
  • web.xml: filter plus filter-mapping with dispatcher children.
  • Programmatic: ctx.addFilter with addMappingForUrlPatterns(types, isMatchAfter, patterns) in a context listener.
  • Wrappers: extend HttpServletRequestWrapper or HttpServletResponseWrapper.

intermediate.content:
Types of Filters

  • • Authentication Filter – Checks user login and session
  • • Authorization Filter – Validates user roles
  • • Logging Filter – Logs request/response details
  • • Compression Filter – Compresses response data
  • • Encoding Filter – Sets character encoding (UTF-8)
  • • CORS Filter – Handles cross-origin requests

Filter Mapping

• Filters can be mapped using either URL patterns or servlet names.
codeExamples:
<filter>
    <filter-name>LoggingFilter</filter-name>
    <filter-class>com.example.LoggingFilter</filter-class>
</filter>

<filter-mapping>
    <filter-name>LoggingFilter</filter-name>
    <url-pattern>/*</url-pattern>
</filter-mapping>

intermediate.content:
Filter Chain

• When multiple filters are applied, they form a chain.
• Each filter must call chain.doFilter() to pass control to the next filter or servlet.


Important Rule

• If chain.doFilter() is not called, the request will not reach the servlet.

Filter vs Interceptor

Feature Filter Interceptor (Spring)
Technology Servlet API Spring MVC
Execution Before and after servlet Before and after controller method
Access No access to controller Full access to controller & model
Use Cases Cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth) Business-level pre/post processing

expert.content:
Advanced Filter Concepts

Dispatcher Types

Filters can be applied to different dispatcher types:

  • • REQUEST – Direct client requests
  • • FORWARD – When RequestDispatcher.forward() is called
  • • INCLUDE – When RequestDispatcher.include() is called
  • • ERROR – On error page handling
  • • ASYNC – For asynchronous processing

Response Wrapping

• Filters can wrap HttpServletResponse to modify output, headers, or content.


Asynchronous Filters

• Use asyncSupported=true for non-blocking processing of requests.


Spring Boot Filters

• In Spring Boot, filters can be registered via @Component or FilterRegistrationBean.

Advanced Security and Performance Practices

  • • Centralize authentication and authorization in filters
  • • Validate input to prevent XSS and SQL injection
  • • Compress and cache responses for performance
  • • Keep filter logic lightweight to reduce overhead
  • • Use filter order to control execution sequence

Mid-Level Notes

  • doFilter receives request, response and FilterChain; calling chain.doFilter(req, resp) passes control on.
  • Not calling the chain blocks the request, which is how an authentication filter rejects a user.
  • Dispatchers: by default filters run for REQUEST only; add FORWARD, INCLUDE, ERROR or ASYNC when needed.

Senior Notes

  • Order: with web.xml the order of filter-mapping elements decides; with annotations the order is not defined by the spec, so use web.xml when order matters.
  • Wrapping: HttpServletRequestWrapper and HttpServletResponseWrapper let a filter change headers or buffer the body for later filters and the servlet.
  • Cross-cutting: keep filters small and stateless, and put business rules in services, not in filters.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting chain.doFilter: the page is blank or 200 with no body.
  • Reading the body twice: the stream can be read once; wrap and cache it.
  • Writing after commit: setting headers after the servlet wrote output has no effect.
  • Casting blindly to HttpServletRequest for non-HTTP requests.
  • Assuming annotation order for security filters.
  • Swallowing exceptions and returning 200.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance advice:

  • Narrow mappings: do not map heavy filters to /* when static files do not need them.
  • No blocking calls (remote auth) on each request without caching.
  • Buffering wrappers cost memory; use them only for the URLs that need them.
  • Order cheap checks first: reject early, before expensive filters.
  • Compression: let the server or proxy gzip when it can.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A typical production filter stack, outermost first:

  • Request id and logging (puts an id in the log context).
  • CORS (answers preflight early).
  • Encoding.
  • Authentication, then authorization.
  • Rate limit or metrics.

beginner.content:
What is Filter Lifecycle?

• Every filter in the Java Servlet API follows a defined lifecycle managed by the servlet container.


Main Lifecycle Methods

  • • init() – Called once when the filter is created. Used for initialization.
  • • doFilter() – Called for every request/response that matches the filter mapping.
  • • destroy() – Called once when the filter is removed or application shuts down.

Execution Flow

• Container creates filter → init() → doFilter() (per request) → destroy() (on shutdown)

Fresher Notes

  • init runs once when the container creates the filter, before it handles any request.
  • doFilter runs for every matching request, often by many threads at the same time.
  • destroy runs once when the application stops, so close resources there.

Worked Example 1

Unsafe shared field.

Worked Example 2

Safe version.

Practice Exercise 1

A filter with all three methods.

Practice Exercise 2

Observing the order.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container manages the filter instance.

  • Create and init: at deployment it calls the no-arg constructor, then init(FilterConfig) once.
  • Service: one shared instance receives concurrent doFilter calls from the request thread pool.
  • Destroy: on undeploy it waits for running calls to finish (or for a timeout), then calls destroy once.
  • Order of init: follows declaration order; destroy follows the reverse.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Lifecycle-related options:

  • init-param: per-filter settings from annotation or web.xml.
  • Context: config.getServletContext() for shared objects.
  • Lazy init: do heavy work in the first call guarded by a lock, only if startup time matters.
  • async-supported: required if the chain uses async processing.

intermediate.content:
init() Method

• Called once when the filter is first instantiated by the servlet container.

  • • Used to read configuration parameters from web.xml or annotations.
  • • Set up resources like database connections, loggers, or cache.

Example

doFilter() Method

• Called for every request and response that matches the filter mapping.
• It can perform pre-processing and post-processing.


Pre-processing

  • • Logging request data
  • • Authentication checks
  • • Encoding setup

Post-processing

  • • Compressing response
  • • Adding custom headers
  • • Logging response time

destroy() Method

• Called once when the filter is removed or the application shuts down.
• Used to release resources acquired in init().

  • • Close database connections
  • • Clear caches
  • • Release file handles or threads

expert.content:
Advanced Lifecycle Concepts

1. Filter Initialization Order

  • • Order defined in web.xml execution order
  • • @WebFilter annotations execute based on container scanning order

2. Async Filters

• Filters can be async-supported to process asynchronous requests (asyncSupported=true). Lifecycle methods remain the same.


3. Resource Management

  • • Use init() to allocate heavy resources once
  • • Always release in destroy() to prevent memory leaks
  • • doFilter() should be lightweight to handle high throughput

4. Error Handling in Lifecycle

  • • Exceptions in init() prevent filter from being registered
  • • Exceptions in doFilter() can propagate to error pages
  • • destroy() should handle exceptions gracefully

Best Practices

  • • Keep init() minimal; avoid heavy processing here
  • • Use doFilter() for per-request logic only
  • • Release all resources in destroy() to prevent leaks
  • • Always call chain.doFilter() unless intentionally blocking request
  • • Use logging to monitor filter lifecycle events for debugging

Mid-Level Notes

  • One instance of each filter exists per declaration, so instance fields are shared between all requests.
  • FilterConfig given to init gives getInitParameter and getServletContext.
  • Default methods: in Servlet 4.0+ init and destroy are default methods, so implement only what you need.

Senior Notes

  • Thread safety: keep per-request data in local variables or request attributes, never in filter fields without synchronization.
  • Fail fast: throw ServletException from init if configuration is missing; the filter is then not put in service.
  • Stack order: the code after chain.doFilter runs in reverse order of the filters before it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Per-request state in fields causes data leaks between users.
  • Resources not closed in destroy.
  • Heavy work in init that blocks deployment on a slow remote service.
  • Assuming one init per request.
  • Swallowing exceptions from init, so the filter runs half configured.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Lifecycle tuning:

  • Build once: compile regexes, parse config and create clients in init.
  • Immutable fields: final fields need no locks.
  • Graceful stop: flush buffers and close clients in destroy.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real case: an audit filter that opens a file or queue client at start and closes it at stop.

  • init: create the writer.
  • doFilter: write one line after the chain, with status and duration.
  • destroy: flush and close.

beginner.content:
What is an Authentication Filter?

• An Authentication Filter is a servlet filter that checks if a user is logged in before allowing access to protected resources.


Purpose

  • • Prevent unauthorized access
  • • Redirect unauthenticated users to login page
  • • Centralize authentication logic

Fresher Notes

  • Idea: a filter checks the session for a logged-in user and redirects to the login page when it is missing.
  • getSession(false) returns null instead of creating a new session, which is what a check needs.
  • Redirect: resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/login").

Worked Example 1

Role filter for admin pages.

Worked Example 2

JSON 401 for APIs.

Practice Exercise 1

Login check filter.

Practice Exercise 2

Login servlet storing the user.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Flow of an authentication filter:

  • Request arrives with a JSESSIONID cookie, or none.
  • Lookup: getSession(false) finds the server-side session, if any.
  • Decision: a user attribute means pass on through the chain; otherwise redirect or send 401.
  • Login: the login servlet verifies the credentials and stores the user, which marks the session as authenticated.
  • Logout: invalidate() removes the session, so the next request fails the check.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants:

  • Session-based: as above, the classic approach for server-rendered pages.
  • Token-based: read Authorization: Bearer ... and validate a JWT or an opaque token.
  • Basic auth: decode the Authorization: Basic header; only safe over HTTPS.
  • Remember-me: a signed long-lived cookie that recreates the session.
  • Container security: security-constraint and login-config in web.xml.

intermediate.content:
Enhancing Authentication Filter

We can enhance the filter by:

  • • Checking user roles (authorization)
  • • Allowing public URLs to bypass authentication
  • • Logging authentication attempts

expert.content:
Advanced Authentication Filter

1. JWT Authentication

• Use filters to validate JSON Web Tokens (JWT) in HTTP headers.


2. Security Best Practices

  • • Always invalidate sessions on logout
  • • Use HTTPS to prevent token/session hijacking
  • • Log authentication failures for monitoring
  • • Keep filter lightweight for performance

3. Spring Boot Integration

• In Spring Boot, authentication filters can be registered via FilterRegistrationBean or @Component.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Public URLs: the login page, static files and the login POST must be excluded, or the user can never log in (redirect loop).
  • Authorization is a second step: after "who are you", check "may you do this", for example a role in the session.
  • Session fixation: after a successful login call request.changeSessionId() to issue a new session id.

Senior Notes

  • API clients do not follow login redirects; return 401 with WWW-Authenticate or a JSON error for /api/*.
  • Prefer the container: for real security use container security or a framework (Spring Security) and treat a hand-made filter as a learning or small-app tool.
  • Cache: add Cache-Control: no-store on protected pages so the browser back button does not show them after logout.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Redirect loop: the login page is protected.
  • getSession() instead of getSession(false) creates sessions for everyone.
  • Trusting a client flag (a hidden field or cookie holding the role).
  • No HTTPS, so the session cookie can be stolen; set Secure and HttpOnly.
  • Plain-text passwords; store a salted hash such as bcrypt.
  • Session fixation not handled.
  • Open redirect from an unchecked next parameter.
codeExamples:
<session-config>
  <cookie-config>
    <http-only>true</http-only>
    <secure>true</secure>
  </cookie-config>
</session-config>

// OUTPUT:
// Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=...; Path=/app; Secure; HttpOnly (id varies)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and robustness:

  • Cheap check first: a session attribute lookup is fast; do not query the database on each request.
  • Cache tokens: keep validated tokens in a small expiring cache.
  • Skip static files with a narrow mapping.
  • No-store headers on protected pages.
  • Timeouts: a sensible session-timeout bounds memory.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an intranet app with user and admin areas.

  • AuthFilter on /* with a public list.
  • AdminFilter on /admin/* checks the role.
  • Audit: log denied attempts with user and path.
  • Migration: move to a framework when requirements grow (SSO, MFA).

beginner.content:
What is ServletContextListener?

• ServletContextListener is an interface in the Servlet API that allows you to listen to lifecycle events of a web application's context.


Purpose

  • • Execute code when the web application starts or stops
  • • Initialize shared resources like database connections
  • • Clean up resources on shutdown

Fresher Notes

  • ServletContextListener gets contextInitialized at startup and contextDestroyed at shutdown of the web application.
  • Register it with @WebListener on the class, or with a listener element in web.xml.
  • Typical jobs: load configuration, create a connection pool, start a scheduler, and clean up at the end.

Worked Example 1

Read config in a servlet.

Worked Example 2

web.xml registration.
codeExamples:
<listener>
  <listener-class>com.example.AppBootstrap</listener-class>
</listener>
<context-param>
  <param-name>jdbcUrl</param-name>
  <param-value>jdbc:mysql://localhost/shop</param-value>
</context-param>

// OUTPUT:
// context-param is read with ctx.getInitParameter("jdbcUrl")

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Startup and shutdown with a pool.

Practice Exercise 2

A scheduler stopped on shutdown.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container notifies listeners around the context lifecycle.

  • Discovery: from @WebListener, web.xml and fragments.
  • Startup: contextInitialized runs before filters and loadOnStartup servlets are initialized.
  • Shutdown: servlets and filters are destroyed first, then contextDestroyed in reverse listener order.
  • Event: ServletContextEvent.getServletContext() gives the shared context.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Related listener types:

  • ServletContextAttributeListener: attribute added, replaced, removed.
  • HttpSessionListener: session created or destroyed.
  • ServletRequestListener: every request starts and ends.
  • Programmatic API: ServletContainerInitializer and ctx.addServlet for framework-style bootstrap.
  • Init params: read context-param values with getInitParameter.

intermediate.content:
Use Cases of ServletContextListener

  • • Initialize database connection pool at startup
  • • Load configuration settings into memory
  • • Initialize logging frameworks
  • • Perform cleanup operations at application shutdown

Accessing ServletContext Attributes

• Attributes set in contextInitialized() can be accessed by any servlet or JSP using ServletContext.getAttribute().

expert.content:
Advanced ServletContextListener Concepts

1. Integration with Filters and Servlets

• ServletContextListener can initialize resources before any servlet or filter is executed.


2. Resource Management

  • • Open database connections in contextInitialized()
  • • Close connections in contextDestroyed()
  • • Initialize caches and logging frameworks

3. Ordering Listeners

• Multiple listeners are executed in the order they are defined in web.xml or based on @WebListener scanning.


4. Best Practices

  • • Keep initialization lightweight to avoid slow startup
  • • Handle exceptions gracefully during startup
  • • Use context attributes to share resources across the application
  • • Always clean up resources to prevent memory leaks

Example: Database Connection Pool

• Initialize a connection pool at startup and store it in ServletContext.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Share objects by storing them in the context: sce.getServletContext().setAttribute("ds", ds), and read them in servlets.
  • Runs first: context listeners are initialized before filters and servlets, so resources are ready for them.
  • Shutdown order: contextDestroyed is called in reverse order of registration.

Senior Notes

  • Leaks on redeploy: threads, JDBC drivers and executors that you start must be stopped in contextDestroyed, or the old class loader stays in memory.
  • Fail fast: an exception in contextInitialized stops the application from starting, which is good for missing configuration.
  • Dependency injection: in a CDI or Spring setup prefer managed beans, and use the listener only for bootstrap.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Not stopping threads on destroy, which leaks the class loader on redeploy.
  • Catching and hiding startup errors, so the app starts broken.
  • Slow startup work that makes the deployment time out.
  • Static singletons that survive a hot redeploy of the class loader.
  • Using the listener for request work.
  • Not deregistering JDBC drivers in container-less pools.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Fast startup: start slow loads on a background thread and expose readiness through /health.
  • Pool sizes from context-param, not constants.
  • Lazy singletons for rarely used services.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: an app that needs a pool, a scheduler and a feature flags map.

  • Start: create the pool, run migrations, schedule jobs.
  • Share: keep services in the context.
  • Stop: stop jobs, then close the pool.

beginner.content:
What is HttpSessionListener?

• HttpSessionListener is an interface in the Java Servlet API that allows you to listen to lifecycle events of HTTP sessions.


Purpose

  • • Track creation and destruction of sessions
  • • Monitor user activity
  • • Perform cleanup when session expires

Session Lifecycle Events

  • • sessionCreated – triggered when a session is created.
  • • sessionDestroyed – triggered when a session is invalidated or times out.

Fresher Notes

  • HttpSessionListener gets sessionCreated and sessionDestroyed when a session starts and ends.
  • Active users are counted by adding one on create and subtracting one on destroy.
  • Register with @WebListener or the listener element in web.xml.

Worked Example 1

Setting the timeout.
codeExamples:
<session-config>
  <session-timeout>15</session-timeout>   <!-- minutes -->
</session-config>

// OUTPUT:
// idle sessions are destroyed after 15 minutes and sessionDestroyed runs

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Logout invalidates.

Practice Exercise 1

Online users counter.

Practice Exercise 2

Showing it in a JSP.
codeExamples:
Users online: ${applicationScope.activeSessions}

// OUTPUT: // Users online: 2

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Session events come from the session manager.

  • Create: getSession(true), or a JSP page with sessions enabled, builds a session and fires sessionCreated.
  • Destroy: invalidate() or a background expiry thread fires sessionDestroyed.
  • Expiry check in Tomcat runs about once a minute, so timeouts are not instantaneous.
  • Event: HttpSessionEvent.getSession() gives the session; in destroy its attributes are still readable.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options and related APIs:

  • sessionIdChanged: from HttpSessionIdListener, fires after changeSessionId.
  • HttpSessionAttributeListener: add, replace, remove events.
  • HttpSessionBindingListener: valueBound and valueUnbound on the value object.
  • Timeout: setMaxInactiveInterval(seconds); a negative value means never.
  • HttpSessionActivationListener: for sessions that are passivated or moved between nodes.

intermediate.content:
Use Cases of HttpSessionListener

  • • Count active users
  • • Invalidate sessions on logout or timeout
  • • Cleanup user-specific resources
  • • Log session events for auditing
  • • Track session creation time for monitoring

Session Timeout Handling

• Sessions can expire automatically after a configured timeout.
• HttpSessionListener can detect this and perform cleanup.

  • • Defined via web.xml or programmatically
  • • Useful for releasing session-specific resources
codeExamples:
<session-config>
    <session-timeout>15</session-timeout> <!-- in minutes -->
</session-config>

intermediate.content:
Tracking Session Attributes

• HttpSessionListener can be combined with HttpSessionAttributeListener to monitor user attributes added or removed during a session.

expert.content:
Advanced Concepts

1. Session Attribute Cleanup

• Use HttpSessionListener to remove sensitive information from memory when a session expires.


2. Distributed/Clustered Environments

• In a cluster, session events may propagate across nodes. Ensure cleanup does not remove active sessions from other nodes.


3. Security Best Practices

  • • Invalidate sessions on logout
  • • Use HTTPS to prevent session hijacking
  • • Limit session lifetime
  • • Monitor unusual session creation/destruction patterns

4. Integration with Filters

• Filters can intercept requests and check session validity, while HttpSessionListener tracks lifecycle events.
Example: Track Active Users and Cleanup

Additional Expert Tips

  • • Combine with HttpSessionBindingListener to monitor individual attribute changes.
  • • Use ConcurrentHashMap or thread-safe collections to track users in multi-threaded environments.
  • • Always handle null session attributes to prevent NullPointerExceptions.
  • • Log session lifecycle events for debugging and auditing purposes.
  • • Use session metadata (creation time, last accessed time) for analytics and monitoring.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Session ends by invalidate() or by timeout, set with session-timeout in minutes in web.xml or setMaxInactiveInterval in seconds.
  • Thread safety: use AtomicInteger for the counter, since many requests create sessions at once.
  • Related listeners: HttpSessionAttributeListener sees attribute changes, and HttpSessionBindingListener is called on the attribute value itself.

Senior Notes

  • Not exact: a count of sessions is not a count of users; one user can have several, and an unseen timeout destroys a session later than the user left.
  • Clusters: a local counter sees only one node, so use a shared store (Redis, database) for a global figure.
  • JSP sessions: JSP pages create a session by default, so crawlers can inflate the count; set session="false" where a session is not needed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Plain int counter: races lose updates; use AtomicInteger.
  • Counting sessions as users.
  • Sessions created by bots or by JSP pages that do not need them.
  • Forgetting the decrement on destroy after a restart (sessions are persisted but the counter is not).
  • Heavy work in the callback blocks the request or the expiry thread.
codeExamples:
<%@ page session="false" %>
<%-- public marketing page: no session, no sessionCreated event --%>

// OUTPUT:
// visiting this page no longer increases the active session count

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Short timeouts for anonymous traffic keep memory low.
  • Small session data: store ids, not big objects.
  • Hand over heavy work to an executor.
  • Shared counters in Redis for clusters.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a dashboard that shows users online, and a cleanup of per-session temp files.

  • Created: increment and publish.
  • Destroyed: delete the temp upload folder of that session.
  • Admin page: read applicationScope.activeSessions.

beginner.content:
What is ServletRequestListener?

• ServletRequestListener is an interface in the Servlet API that allows you to listen to lifecycle events of servlet requests.


Purpose

  • • Monitor when a request is created and destroyed
  • • Useful for logging, analytics, or resource initialization
  • • Track request processing time

Fresher Notes

  • ServletRequestListener is called when a request enters (requestInitialized) and leaves (requestDestroyed) the web application.
  • Registration: annotate the class with @WebListener or declare a <listener> element in web.xml.
  • Event object: ServletRequestEvent gives getServletRequest() and getServletContext().

Worked Example 1

Timing a request.

Worked Example 2

Watch attribute changes.

Practice Exercise 1

Count requests with a listener.

Practice Exercise 2

web.xml registration.
codeExamples:
<listener>
    <listener-class>com.example.CountListener</listener-class>
</listener>

<!-- Same effect as @WebListener;
the class must have a public no-arg constructor -->

// OUTPUT:
// The container instantiates CountListener once at startup and calls it for every request.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The container calls listeners around the request pipeline.

  • Discovery: at startup the container scans for @WebListener classes and reads listener entries, then keeps one instance for each.
  • Order: requestInitialized runs in declaration order, requestDestroyed in reverse order.
  • Timing: initialized fires before the first filter, destroyed after the last filter and servlet have completed.
  • Thread: both calls usually run on the same container thread, but with async they may not.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Related listener interfaces:

  • ServletContextListener: startup and shutdown of the whole application.
  • HttpSessionListener: session create and destroy.
  • ServletRequestAttributeListener: attribute add, remove and replace on requests.
  • AsyncListener: complete, timeout, error and start events of async processing.
  • Registration: annotation, web.xml, or ServletContext.addListener inside a ServletContainerInitializer.

intermediate.content:
Use Cases of ServletRequestListener

  • • Log each incoming HTTP request
  • • Track request processing time
  • • Initialize request-scoped resources
  • • Monitor request counts for analytics

Integration with Filters

• ServletRequestListener works alongside filters to track request lifecycle:

  • • Filters can modify request/response objects
  • • RequestListener monitors overall request lifecycle

expert.content:
Advanced Concepts

1. Request Metrics & Monitoring

• Track concurrent requests, request rate, and processing times for performance monitoring.


2. Resource Management

  • • Initialize request-scoped resources in requestInitialized()
  • • Cleanup in requestDestroyed() to avoid memory leaks

3. Security Applications

  • • Log IP addresses for each request
  • • Detect unusual traffic patterns
  • • Monitor request headers and parameters for auditing

4. Best Practices

  • • Keep listener logic lightweight
  • • Do not perform heavy DB operations in listener
  • • Use thread-safe collections if tracking multiple requests
  • • Combine with filters and session listeners for complete monitoring
Example: Track Request Count and Duration

Mid-Level Notes

  • Cast needed: cast the request to HttpServletRequest to read the URI, method and headers.
  • Attribute listener: ServletRequestAttributeListener reports setAttribute, replace and remove on a request.
  • Use cases: request logging, timing, a correlation id, and cleaning per-request resources.

Senior Notes

  • Cross-cutting: a Filter is better for changing the request or response; a listener only observes lifecycle events.
  • Thread context: set and clear a logging context (MDC) in the pair of methods so thread-pool threads never leak data.
  • Async: with startAsync the request is destroyed only when the async cycle completes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common mistakes:

  • Storing request data in a field: the listener is shared, so a field is overwritten by concurrent requests; use a request attribute.
  • Heavy work: slow code in requestInitialized delays every request.
  • Not casting: forgetting that the request is a ServletRequest and not an HttpServletRequest.
  • Missing cleanup: a ThreadLocal set in initialized but not cleared in destroyed.
  • Wrong class: a listener without a public no-arg constructor fails at startup.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance and tuning:

  • Cost: the listener runs for every request, including static files, so keep it to a few microseconds.
  • Logging: use asynchronous appenders and avoid string building when the level is disabled.
  • Counters: use AtomicLong or LongAdder, not synchronized blocks.
  • Filter alternative: a filter with a url pattern can skip static resources.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: add a correlation id to every log line for support tracing.

  • Start: read X-Request-Id or generate one, put it in the MDC.
  • End: clear the MDC so the pooled thread is clean.
  • Result: logs from one request are searchable by one id.

beginner.content:
What are Error Pages?

• In Java web applications, error pages are custom pages that are displayed when a server-side error occurs (like 404 Not Found or 500 Internal Server Error).
• Instead of showing default server errors, you can define user-friendly pages using web.xml.


Common HTTP errors to handle:

  • • 400 - Bad Request
  • • 401 - Unauthorized
  • • 403 - Forbidden
  • • 404 - Not Found
  • • 500 - Internal Server Error
codeExamples:
<error-page>
                    <error-code>404</error-code>
                    <location>/errors/404.html</location>
                </error-page>

                <error-page>
                    <exception-type>java.lang.Throwable</exception-type>
                    <location>/errors/error.html</location>
                </error-page>

beginner.content:
Simple HTML Error Page Example

Beginner-friendly static HTML error page:
codeExamples:
404 Error

The page you requested does not exist.

Go to Home

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • error-page element in web.xml maps an HTTP status code or an exception type to a page, servlet or JSP.
  • By status: <error-code>404</error-code> plus <location>/errors/404.jsp</location>.
  • By exception: <exception-type>java.lang.Exception</exception-type> catches uncaught exceptions from servlets.

Worked Example 1

Read the error attributes.
codeExamples:
<%@ page isErrorPage="true" contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %>

Error <%= request.getAttribute("javax.servlet.error.status_code") %>

URL: <%= request.getAttribute("javax.servlet.error.request_uri") %>

Type: <%= request.getAttribute("javax.servlet.error.exception_type") %>

// OUTPUT: (rendered, varies) // Error 500 // URL: /shop/order // Type: class java.lang.NullPointerException

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Trigger an error from a servlet.

Practice Exercise 1

Error pages in web.xml.
codeExamples:
<error-page>
    <error-code>404</error-code>
    <location>/errors/404.jsp</location>
</error-page>
<error-page>
    <error-code>500</error-code>
    <location>/errors/500.jsp</location>
</error-page>
<error-page>
    <exception-type>java.lang.NullPointerException</exception-type>
    <location>/errors/npe.jsp</location>
</error-page>

// OUTPUT:
// GET /missing  -> HTTP 404, body from /errors/404.jsp
// NullPointerException in a servlet -> HTTP 500, body from /errors/npe.jsp

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

A catch-all page.
codeExamples:
<error-page>
    <location>/errors/generic.jsp</location>
</error-page>

<!-- Servlet 3.0+: used when no code or exception entry matches -->

// OUTPUT:
// GET /api/x returns 405 with no matching entry -> /errors/generic.jsp

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

When an error happens, the container runs an error dispatch.

  • Trigger: sendError, an uncaught exception, or a status such as 404 produced by the container.
  • Lookup: first the exception type (walking up the class hierarchy, also checking the root cause of a ServletException), then the status code, then the default entry.
  • Dispatch: the response buffer is reset, the attributes are set, and the page is invoked with dispatcher type ERROR.
  • Attributes: javax.servlet.error.status_code, exception_type, message, exception, request_uri, servlet_name.
codeExamples:
<error-page>
    <exception-type>java.io.IOException</exception-type>
    <location>/errors/io.jsp</location>
</error-page>
<error-page>
    <exception-type>java.lang.Throwable</exception-type>
    <location>/errors/any.jsp</location>
</error-page>

// OUTPUT:
// FileNotFoundException (subclass of IOException) -> /errors/io.jsp
// IllegalStateException                           -> /errors/any.jsp

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants of the mapping:

  • error-code: any valid HTTP status, for example 400, 403, 404, 405, 500, 503.
  • exception-type: a fully qualified class name.
  • location: must begin with a slash and can be a JSP, HTML file or servlet path.
  • Default: an entry without code or type.
  • Spring Boot: embedded containers use /error and ErrorController instead of web.xml.
codeExamples:
<error-page>
    <error-code>403</error-code>
    <location>/errors/forbidden.html</location>
</error-page>
<error-page>
    <error-code>503</error-code>
    <location>/errors/maintenance.html</location>
</error-page>

// OUTPUT:
// HTTP 403 shows forbidden.html; HTTP 503 shows maintenance.html (static files work too)

intermediate.content:
Configuring Multiple Error Pages

• You can configure multiple error pages for different HTTP codes and exceptions.
• This helps in providing tailored messages for different situations.
codeExamples:
<error-page>
                    <error-code>403</error-code>
                    <location>/errors/403.html</location>
                </error-page>
                
                <error-page>
                    <error-code>500</error-code>
                    <location>/errors/serverError.jsp</location>
                </error-page>
                
                <error-page>
                    <exception-type>java.lang.NullPointerException</exception-type>
                    <location>/errors/npe.jsp</location>
                </error-page>

intermediate.content:
Dynamic Error Messages in JSP

• JSP error pages can use EL (Expression Language) and JSP tags to show dynamic details:
codeExamples:
<%@ page isErrorPage="true" %>

Error Details

Status Code: {"$"request.getAttribute("jakarta.servlet.error.status_code")}

Error Message: {"$"request.getAttribute("jakarta.servlet.error.message")}

Exception: {"$"exception}

intermediate.content:
Forwarding vs Redirecting on Errors

• Forwarding: The URL in the browser remains the same; server internally forwards to error page.
• Redirecting: Browser is sent a redirect response; URL changes. Forwarding is preferred for consistent error handling.

expert.content:
Centralized Servlet Error Handling

Experts use a dedicated servlet for all exceptions. Benefits:

  • • Centralized logging
  • • Custom response codes and messages
  • • Conditional error pages based on exception type
codeExamples:
<error-page>
                    <exception-type>java.lang.Throwable</exception-type>
                    <location>/ErrorHandlerServlet</location>
                </error-page>
                
                // ErrorHandlerServlet.java
                protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response)
                        throws ServletException, IOException {
                    Integer statusCode = (Integer) request.getAttribute("jakarta.servlet.error.status_code");
                    Throwable throwable = (Throwable) request.getAttribute("jakarta.servlet.error.exception");

                    if (statusCode == 404) {
                        request.getRequestDispatcher("/errors/404.jsp").forward(request, response);
                    } else if (throwable instanceof NullPointerException) {
                        request.getRequestDispatcher("/errors/npe.jsp").forward(request, response);
                    } else {
                        request.getRequestDispatcher("/errors/generalError.jsp").forward(request, response);
                    }

                    logger.error("Error occurred: Status={}, Exception={}", statusCode, throwable);
                }

expert.content:
Best Practices for Error Pages

  • • Always provide navigation links to home or main sections.
  • • Do not reveal stack traces or sensitive information to users.
  • • Log detailed error information on the server.
  • • Use consistent design for all error pages for better UX.
  • • Test error pages by simulating errors (e.g., throw exceptions in servlets).

Integration with Logging Frameworks

• Integrate with frameworks like log4j or SLF4J to log all errors from error handling servlets or JSP pages.
• This helps in monitoring production issues effectively.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Request attributes: the container sets javax.servlet.error.status_code, exception_type, message, exception and request_uri (Jakarta EE 9+ uses jakarta.servlet.error.*).
  • Most specific wins: an exact exception type beats its superclass, and a status code entry is used when no exception entry matches.
  • Default page: an error-page with neither code nor type (Servlet 3.0+) is the catch-all.

Senior Notes

  • Status preserved: the container keeps the original status code when it dispatches to the error page, unless the page changes it.
  • Committed response: if the response is already committed, the error page cannot be shown, so buffer output and handle errors early.
  • Security: never print stack traces to users; log them and show a reference id.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Location without slash: the path is rejected at startup; always start with /.
  • Error page throws: keep it simple and avoid dependencies that can fail.
  • Wrong attribute prefix: on Jakarta EE 9+ use jakarta.servlet.error.*.
  • Duplicate entries: two entries for the same code or type make deployment fail.
  • Small body in IE: old browsers replace error bodies shorter than 512 bytes.
  • Leaking details: printing the stack trace exposes class names and paths.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Static error pages: HTML files are cheap and have no failure path.
  • Cache headers: set Cache-Control: no-store on dynamic error output.
  • Bots: many 404s from scanners can flood logs, so log them at a lower level.
  • Status integrity: do not turn errors into 200, because proxies and monitoring rely on the status.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a storefront needs a branded 404, a maintenance page and no stack traces.

  • 404: static page with search box and links.
  • 500: servlet that logs and shows a reference id.
  • 503: static maintenance page, usable even when the database is down.
codeExamples:
<error-page><error-code>404</error-code><location>/errors/404.html</location></error-page>
<error-page><error-code>500</error-code><location>/error</location></error-page>
<error-page><error-code>503</error-code><location>/errors/maint.html</location></error-page>
<error-page><location>/error</location></error-page>

// OUTPUT:
// /nope -> 404.html, DB outage -> 500 via /error with id, deploy window -> 503 page

beginner.content:
What is Custom Error Handling?

• Custom error handling allows developers to manage errors gracefully in their applications instead of letting the program crash.
• It helps in giving meaningful messages to the user and logging errors for debugging.

• In Java, we usually create custom exceptions by extending the Exception class.

Why use custom exceptions?

  • • Provide meaningful error messages to users
  • • Differentiate between different types of errors
  • • Enable better debugging and logging
  • • Make your code more readable and maintainable

Fresher Notes

  • Custom error handling means showing friendly pages and logging details instead of the raw container stack trace.
  • sendError: response.sendError(404, "msg") triggers the matching error page; setStatus does not.
  • Error servlet: the location can be a servlet that reads the error attributes and builds the response.

Worked Example 1

Forward to a friendly page.

Worked Example 2

JSON for API paths.

Practice Exercise 1

Error servlet with log id.

Practice Exercise 2

Page-level error handling.
codeExamples:
<%-- order.jsp --%> <%@ page errorPage="/errors/page-error.jsp" %> <% int qty = Integer.parseInt(request.getParameter("qty")); %> <%-- page-error.jsp --%> <%@ page isErrorPage="true" %>

Bad input: <%= exception.getMessage() %>

// OUTPUT: (qty=abc) // Bad input: For input string: "abc"

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Custom handling works at several layers.

  • Code level: try-catch in servlets decides the status and view.
  • Page level: the errorPage attribute makes the JSP catch its own exception and forward to the error JSP, which sets the exception variable.
  • Container level: error-page entries handle whatever escapes.
  • Framework level: filters or advice objects can convert exceptions before the container sees them.
codeExamples:
<%-- generated code idea inside _jspService --%>
try {
    // page body
} catch (Throwable t) {
    if (pageContext != null) pageContext.handlePageException(t);
}

// OUTPUT:
// handlePageException forwards to the errorPage JSP with the exception in the request

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options for choosing the response:

  • sendError(code): container error page, resets the buffer.
  • setStatus plus body: you own the page, the container does not intervene.
  • Redirect: use for post-redirect-get, not for errors.
  • Forward to view: keeps the URL and request attributes.
  • Filter wrapper: a filter that catches exceptions from chain.doFilter gives one handling place.

intermediate.content:
Handling Multiple Exceptions

• You can create multiple custom exceptions and handle them separately to improve clarity and control.

Using finally block

• The finally block always executes regardless of an exception.
• It is useful for cleaning up resources like files, database connections, etc.

Try-with-resources (Java 7+)

• For resources like streams, files, and connections, Java's try-with-resources automatically closes resources and handles exceptions efficiently.

expert.content:
Advanced Custom Error Handling

Expert-level error handling involves:

  • • Creating a hierarchy of custom exceptions
  • • Logging errors with frameworks (e.g., Log4j, SLF4J)
  • • Using global exception handling in web applications (like Spring Boot @ControllerAdvice)
  • • Recovering from exceptions or fallback mechanisms
  • • Adding error codes and metadata for API responses

Error Logging

• Logging exceptions with frameworks like Log4j or SLF4J is crucial for monitoring and debugging.
• Include exception stack traces, timestamps, and context.

Fallback and Recovery

• In resilient applications, you can implement fallback mechanisms for critical operations.
• For example, using default values, retrying failed operations, or switching to backup services.

Exception Hierarchy Best Practices

  • • Group related exceptions under a common parent
  • • Use checked exceptions for recoverable errors
  • • Use unchecked exceptions for programming errors
  • • Provide meaningful messages and error codes

Mid-Level Notes

  • Page-level: a JSP uses errorPage="/err.jsp" in its page directive, and the target declares isErrorPage="true" to get the exception object.
  • Application-level: web.xml entries apply to all resources and are the default choice.
  • Logging: log the exception with a correlation id and show only that id to the user.

Senior Notes

  • Content negotiation: return JSON for API paths and HTML for browser paths from the same error servlet, using the Accept header or URL prefix.
  • Never swallow: catching an exception and returning 200 hides failures from monitoring and clients.
  • Frameworks: Spring and others add their own handlers (such as @ControllerAdvice) before the container error page runs.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Catch and ignore: add logging and rethrow or send a proper status.
  • Returning 200 for errors: clients cannot tell failure from success.
  • Exposing the message: exception messages may contain SQL or paths.
  • sendError after output: throws IllegalStateException; buffer first.
  • Forgetting isErrorPage: the exception object is null in the target JSP.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning and operations:

  • Log once: log at the point of handling to avoid duplicate stack traces.
  • Rate limits: bursts of the same error should not flood storage.
  • Metrics: count errors by status for alerting.
  • Error budget: alerts on the 5xx rate, not on single failures.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Scenario: a REST plus web application needs both views.

  • Browser paths: HTML page with reference id.
  • API paths: JSON body with code and id.
  • Support: the id lets staff find the log entry.

What is JSP?

JSP (JavaServer Pages) is a server-side technology used to create dynamic web applications using Java.

It allows developers to embed Java code inside HTML pages.

Why JSP?

  • Easy to mix HTML and Java
  • Built on top of Servlet technology
  • Automatically converted into Servlet by the server

  • Lifecycle: translation, compilation, loading, jspInit, _jspService per request, and jspDestroy.
  • First request is slower because the page is translated and compiled; later requests reuse the loaded class.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

JSP runs through a translation pipeline.

  • Translation: Jasper converts the page into a Java source file (Tomcat keeps it under work/Catalina/...): HTML becomes out.write("..."), scriptlets are copied, expressions become out.print(...), declarations become members.
  • Compilation: the source is compiled to a class and loaded by a per-page class loader.
  • Request: _jspService(request, response) runs once per request on many threads.
  • Reload: when the file timestamp changes (development mode), the page is retranslated.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants and configuration:

  • JSP syntax: classic tags or XML form (.jspx).
  • Fragments: .jspf files for includes.
  • Tag files: .tag files define reusable tags in JSP syntax.
  • Jasper options: development, checkInterval, genStringAsCharArray in the JspServlet init-params.
  • Mapping: *.jsp is handled by the built-in JspServlet.
codeExamples:
<servlet>
    <servlet-name>jsp</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>org.apache.jasper.servlet.JspServlet</servlet-class>
    <init-param><param-name>development</param-name><param-value>false</param-value></init-param>
    <init-param><param-name>checkInterval</param-name><param-value>0</param-value></init-param>
</servlet>

// OUTPUT:
// Production: no file timestamp checks, so pages are not retranslated after deployment

MVC Architecture with JSP

In MVC:

  • Model - Java Beans / Business Logic
  • View - JSP
  • Controller - Servlet

Best practice: Use JSP only for view, not for business logic.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Generated servlet: the page becomes a class extending HttpJspBase (Tomcat), with HTML written through out.write.
  • Implicit objects: request, response, session, out, application, config, pageContext, page, exception.
  • Placement: pages under WEB-INF cannot be requested directly, so they are shown only through a servlet forward.

Senior Notes

  • MVC: servlets handle logic (controller), JSP only renders (view), and beans carry the model.
  • Precompile: translate pages at build time (Jasper ant or Maven plugin) to avoid first-hit delay and to find errors early.
  • Thread safety: one servlet instance serves many threads, so declarations (fields) in a page are shared and unsafe.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Business logic in pages: move it to servlets and services.
  • Direct access to private pages: place views under WEB-INF.
  • Wrong encoding: set pageEncoding and contentType to UTF-8.
  • Unescaped output: leads to cross-site scripting.
  • Shared fields: declarations are not thread-safe.
  • Large pages: a method over 64KB fails to compile; split with includes.
codeExamples:
<%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" pageEncoding="UTF-8" %>
<%-- WRONG: <%= request.getParameter("q") %> prints raw input --%>
<%-- RIGHT: use c:out so that markup in q is escaped --%>

// OUTPUT: (q=<script>alert(1)</script>)
// WRONG: the script runs in the browser
// RIGHT: <script>alert(1)</script> is shown as text

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Precompile: avoids first-request latency and moves errors to build time.
  • Buffer: keep the default buffer or increase it for large pages; avoid autoFlush surprises.
  • Whitespace: trimDirectiveWhitespaces reduces output size.
  • session=false where not needed.
  • Caching: cache rendered fragments or use HTTP caching for static parts.
codeExamples:
<%@ page session="false" trimDirectiveWhitespaces="true" buffer="16kb" %>

// OUTPUT:
// No HttpSession is created for this page and blank lines from directives are removed
// (saves memory per visitor and a few bytes per response)

Best Practices

  • Use EL and JSTL over scriptlets for cleaner code.
  • Keep JSP focused on presentation.
  • Use directives and include files for modularity.
  • Precompile JSPs to improve first-load performance.
  • Use session and application objects wisely to avoid memory issues.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Scope of variables: scriptlet variables are local to one request; declaration variables are instance fields shared by all requests.
  • HTML comment <!-- --> is sent to the client, unlike the JSP comment.
  • Directives and actions are other element types: <%@ ... %> and <jsp:... />.

Senior Notes

  • Avoid scriptlets: they mix logic with markup, are hard to test and reuse, and invite XSS; use JSTL and dollar-brace EL instead.
  • Escaping: an expression prints raw text, so user data must be escaped (c:out or fn:escapeXml).
  • Config: scripting-invalid in jsp-config can ban scriptlets for a project.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Semicolon in expression: causes a compile error; remove it.
  • Unbalanced braces: a scriptlet block opened with { must close in a later scriptlet.
  • Declaration used for per-request data: use a scriptlet or an attribute.
  • Raw output of input: escape it.
  • Null printing: an expression returning null prints the text null, so check or use c:out with a default.

<%= name; %>

<%-- RIGHT --%>

<%= name %>

// OUTPUT: // WRONG: JasperException: Unable to compile class for JSP (syntax error on token ";") // RIGHT:

Abaji

Performance and quality:

  • Scriptlet loops over large data are not slower than JSTL, but logic in pages is hard to profile and test.
  • Static text: converted to byte arrays by Jasper, so it is cheap.
  • Database access in a scriptlet: avoid; it blocks rendering and leaks connections on errors.
  • Thread safety: remove mutable declarations.
codeExamples:
<%-- WRONG: connection opened in the page --%>
<% Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(url); /* leaked if an exception occurs */ %>

// RIGHT: DAO in the controller with try-with-resources, page only renders the result.

// OUTPUT:
// Wrong version: connection leak under errors (pool exhausted after many requests)

  • Step 2: pass data as request attributes.
  • Step 3: replace loops with c:forEach and values with EL.
  • Step 4: turn on scripting-invalid to prevent regressions.

Useful page attributes:

  • errorPage, isErrorPage: error handling.

intermediate.content:
1. Page Directive (<%@ page %>)

Used to define page-level properties. Common attributes:

  • language – Java is default (language="java").
  • contentType – MIME type of response (contentType="text/html; charset=UTF-8").
  • session – Enable or disable session (session="true").
  • errorPage – JSP page to handle exceptions (errorPage="error.jsp").
  • buffer – Output buffer size (buffer="16kb").
  • isThreadSafe – Defaults to true (concurrent requests allowed). Setting isThreadSafe="false" makes the container SERIALIZE requests one at a time - it adds queueing, it does not disable protection. Deprecated along with SingleThreadModel; write thread-safe pages instead.

<%@ page language="java" contentType="text/html; charset=UTF-8" session="true" buffer="16kb" errorPage="error.jsp" %>

Advanced Page Directive Attributes

  • isErrorPage – Specifies if the JSP page is an error page (true/false).
  • import – Import Java packages (import="java.util.*,java.sql.*").
  • session – Control session creation (session="false" to disable).

expert.content:
Example Combining All Directives

<%@ page language="java" contentType="text/html; charset=UTF-8" session="true" errorPage="error.jsp" buffer="16kb" import="java.util.*" %>
<%@ include file="header.jsp" %>
<%@ taglib uri="http://java.sun.com/jsp/jstl/core" prefix="c" %>

<html>
<body>
<h2>Combined JSP Directives Demo</h2>
< c:set var="names" value="'$'{['Ashish', 'Raoji', 'Netaji']}" />
< ul >
< c:forEach var="name" items="'$'{names}" >
   < li >'$'{name}
< /c:forEach>
< /ul>
< p >Session ID: <%= session.getId() %>

</body>
</html>

Best Practices for JSP Directives

  • Use page directive to set content type, session, and error pages.
  • Use include directive for static header/footer content; use jsp:include for dynamic content.
  • Always declare JSTL or custom tag libraries with taglib directive to avoid compilation errors.
  • Keep JSP directives at the top of the JSP page for clarity.

Mid-Level Notes

  • import: <%@ page import="java.util.*" %> may appear several times; other attributes may appear only once.
  • include directive is static: the included file is merged before compilation, so it shares variables with the host page.
  • taglib: <%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="..." %>; the URI for JSTL core is http://java.sun.com/jsp/jstl/core (Jakarta: jakarta.tags.core).

Senior Notes

  • Include trade-off: the include directive is fast at runtime but changes in the included file may need a recompile (container dependent); jsp:include is dynamic.
  • session=false on pages that do not need a session avoids creating one needlessly.
  • buffer and autoFlush: the default buffer is 8kb; error pages and forwards only work before the response is committed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes and fixes:

  • Missing taglib: tags print as plain text; declare the prefix.
  • Wrong URI for the server version: javax JSTL and Jakarta JSTL URIs differ.
  • Variable clash with include: a static include shares scope, so duplicate declarations fail to compile.
  • Changed include not visible: some containers do not track dependencies of static includes; touch the host page.
  • Wrong encoding: set pageEncoding as well as contentType.
codeExamples:
<%-- header.jspf --%>
<% int count = 1;
%>
<%-- main.jsp --%>
<%@ include file="header.jspf" %>
<% int count = 2;
%>

// OUTPUT:
// JasperException: Duplicate local variable count (the pages were merged into one method)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tuning:

  • Static include for fixed headers and footers is cheapest at runtime.
  • Prelude and coda avoid repeating directives.
  • session false and buffer choices reduce memory.
  • Tag libraries are cached after first parse; keep the .tld files in a jar for faster scanning, and skip unneeded jar scans with tomcat.util.scan.StandardJarScanFilter.
codeExamples:
<jsp-property-group>
    <url-pattern>*.jsp</url-pattern>
    <include-prelude>/WEB-INF/fragments/prelude.jspf</include-prelude>
    <include-coda>/WEB-INF/fragments/coda.jspf</include-coda>
</jsp-property-group>

// OUTPUT:
// Every page starts with the prelude (taglibs) and ends with the coda (scripts)

beginner.content:
JSP provides standard action tags to simplify common tasks like including pages, forwarding requests, and managing JavaBeans. These tags remove the need for scriptlets (<% %>) and make JSP pages cleaner and easier to maintain.

Common JSP Standard Action Tags:
  • <jsp:include> – Dynamically includes another JSP or HTML page.
  • <jsp:forward> – Forwards the request to another resource (JSP, Servlet, or HTML page).
  • <jsp:param> – Passes parameters along with jsp:include or jsp:forward.
  • <jsp:useBean> – Declares or retrieves a JavaBean for use in JSP.
  • <jsp:setProperty> – Sets property values of a JavaBean.
  • <jsp:getProperty> – Reads property values of a JavaBean and outputs them.
  • <jsp:fallback> – Legal only inside <jsp:plugin>; supplies content for browsers that cannot run the applet/bean plugin. It does NOT catch a failing custom tag - use <c:catch> or a JSP errorPage for that.
codeExamples: <jsp:include page="header.jsp" />
<jsp:forward page="login.jsp" />
<jsp:useBean id="user" class="com.example.User" scope="session" />
<jsp:setProperty name="user" property="name" value="Ashish" />
<jsp:getProperty name="user" property="name" />
